nezeri.q: Which function does a Kotlin program start from?
nezeri.exp: The entry point of every Kotlin program is the main() function. Unlike in Java, it doesn't have to be inside a class — it can live directly in a file.

nezeri.q: Is a semicolon (;) at the end of a line mandatory in Kotlin?
nezeri.exp: The semicolon is optional. You only need it when you write several statements on one line — and that isn't recommended. The only mandatory case: in an enum, when there are additional members after the constants.

nezeri.q: Which function is used to print text to the screen?
nezeri.exp: println() prints the text and moves to a new line, while print() stays on the same line. Both are in the kotlin.io package and are imported automatically.

nezeri.q: How do you write a single-line comment?
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, a single-line comment is written with //, and a block comment with /* ... */. For documentation, /** ... */ (KDoc) is used.

nezeri.q: What does this code print?
nezeri.exp: println() adds a line break at the end, while print() doesn't. That's why "Salam" appears on its own line and "AB" comes out joined together.

nezeri.q: Where in the file is the package declaration written?
opts: At the very top, before the imports
nezeri.exp: The package declaration must be the first meaningful line of the file — only comments and file annotations can come before it. The imports are written after it.

nezeri.q: Can block comments be nested in Kotlin?
nezeri.exp: Yes — in Kotlin, /* /* nested */ */ works correctly. In Java this isn't possible and causes a compilation error.

nezeri.q: Which of the following is a correct function declaration?
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, a function is declared with the fun keyword. The return type is written after the function name and parameters, following a colon: fun ad(): Int.

nezeri.q: How do you insert a variable into a string template?
nezeri.exp: For a simple variable you use $ad, and for an expression the ${ad.length} form. If you need an actual $ character, write \$.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
opts: Kotlin dilinin adında ad.length hərf var
nezeri.exp: $ad substitutes a simple variable, while ${ad.length} evaluates the expression inside the braces and inserts its result. The word "Kotlin" has 6 letters.

nezeri.q: What is if in Kotlin?
opts: Both a statement and an expression that returns a value
Only a statement, like in Java
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, if returns a value: val maks = if (a > b) a else b. That's exactly why the language has no ternary operator (? :) — there's no need for it.

nezeri.q: Is the else branch mandatory in an if used as an expression?
nezeri.exp: An expression must always return a value. Without else, it would be unknown which value to return when the condition is false — that's why the compiler requires else.

nezeri.q: Which packages are imported automatically into every Kotlin file?
nezeri.exp: kotlin.*, kotlin.collections.*, kotlin.io.*, kotlin.text.*, kotlin.ranges.* and, on the JVM, java.lang.* are included automatically. println, listOf, String — they all come from here.

nezeri.q: What does the line import kotlin.math.max as boyuk do?
opts: Lets you refer to the max function by the name boyuk
It's an error — you can't use as
nezeri.exp: The as keyword creates an alias (a rename) for an import. This is especially useful when elements with the same name come from two different packages.

nezeri.q: Is it mandatory to write the return type in a single-expression function?
nezeri.code: fun kvadrat(x: Int) = x * x
opts: No, the compiler infers it itself
nezeri.exp: In a single-expression function (written with =), type inference works. But in a public API it's recommended to write the type explicitly — it improves readability and guards against accidental changes.

nezeri.q: Does this code compile?
opts: No, try can't be an expression
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, try is an expression too and returns a value. Since "42".toInt() succeeds, the last expression of the try block — that is, 42 — is returned.

nezeri.q: Which naming style is recommended for class names?
nezeri.exp: Classes and interfaces are written in PascalCase (IstifadeciProfili), functions and variables in camelCase (hesablaCemi), and top-level consts in SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE (MAX_OLCU).

nezeri.q: Do these two functions do the same thing?
nezeri.code:

fun b(x: Int) = x + 1
opts: No, b() doesn't return a value
nezeri.exp: The single-expression form is just a shorthand. The compiler generates the same bytecode for both; the return type of b() is inferred as Int.

nezeri.q: In the main(args: Array<String>) form, what does args represent?
nezeri.exp: args holds the command-line arguments passed when the program is launched. If you don't need arguments, writing main() without parameters is enough.

nezeri.q: When is a semicolon mandatory in an enum?
opts: When there are additional members (functions, properties) after the constants
nezeri.exp: The semicolon is needed to separate the list of constants from the rest of the class body. If there are only constants, it isn't required.

nezeri.q: What do you do to use spaces in test function names?
nezeri.exp: Inside backticks, Kotlin names can contain spaces and special characters: fun `bos siyahi 0 qaytarir`() { }. This makes tests read like sentences and is mainly used in test code.

nezeri.exp: @file:JvmName("Komekciler") is written at the very top of the file and makes the name visible from Java Komekciler instead of KomekcilerKt.

opts: No, everything must be in a class
Yes, functions can live directly in a file
nezeri.exp: This is an important difference between Kotlin and Java. Functions and properties can be declared directly in a file; on the JVM they become static members of the FaylAdiKt class.

nezeri.q: What's the difference between val and var?
opts: val can't be changed, var can
var is only used inside a class
nezeri.exp: val is a read-only reference — once it's assigned, it can't be reassigned. var, on the other hand, can be changed. It's recommended to always start with val.

nezeri.q: What is the default type for whole numbers?
nezeri.exp: When you write val x = 42, the compiler picks the Int type (32 bits). If the value is larger than the Int range, it automatically becomes Long.

nezeri.q: What is the default type for decimal numbers?
nezeri.exp: In val pi = 3.14, the type is Double (64 bits). To get a Float you need the f suffix: 3.14f.

nezeri.q: Does this code work?
nezeri.code:
val ad = "Kotlin"
ad = "Java"
opts: No — a val can't be reassigned
nezeri.exp: val is read-only. If you need to change the value, you should use var.

nezeri.q: Which quotes are used to write the Char type?
nezeri.exp: A Char is written in single quotes ('A'), and a String in double quotes ("A"). In Kotlin these are different types.

nezeri.q: What does the underscore do in 1_000_000?
opts: It's only for readability and doesn't affect the value
nezeri.exp: The underscore makes large numbers readable. The compiler ignores it completely — 1_000_000 and 1000000 are the same value.

nezeri.q: Which values does the Boolean type accept?
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, Boolean accepts only true and false. Unlike in C, a number can't be used as a Boolean.

nezeri.q: Which function is used to convert text to a number?
nezeri.exp: "42".toInt() converts the text to an Int. If the conversion fails, a NumberFormatException is thrown — the safe option is toIntOrNull().

nezeri.q: Which number system is the 0xFF literal in?
nezeri.exp: The 0x prefix indicates the hexadecimal system. 0xFF equals 255 in decimal. For binary, the 0b prefix is used.

nezeri.q: Does this code compile?
nezeri.code:
val x: Int = 10
val y: Long = x
opts: No — an explicit conversion is needed: x.toLong()
Yes, but the value is lost
Only when x is a constant
nezeri.exp: Kotlin doesn't do automatic number conversions — an important difference from Java. This prevents hidden data loss. You have to write x.toLong() explicitly.

nezeri.q: What is the result of the expression 7 / 2?
nezeri.exp: Since both operands are Int, integer division is performed and the fractional part is dropped. For a decimal result, at least one of them must be a Double: 7.0 / 2 → 3.5.

nezeri.q: What does "abc".toIntOrNull() return?
nezeri.exp: When the conversion isn't possible, toIntOrNull() doesn't throw an exception — it returns null. This is the safest approach when processing user input.

nezeri.q: What's the difference between const val and a regular val?
opts: const val is a compile-time constant and can only be a primitive/String
const val takes up more memory
const val only exists inside a class
nezeri.exp: The value of a const val must be known at compile time, and it can only be declared at the top level or inside an object or companion object. For values computed at runtime, a regular val is used.

nezeri.q: Which types does lateinit NOT work with?
nezeri.exp: lateinit doesn't work with primitive types, because they have no internal null value to represent the "not assigned yet" state. For that, by Delegates.notNull() is used.

nezeri.q: When is by lazy evaluated?
opts: Once on first access, then it's cached
nezeri.exp: by lazy computes the value on the first read and stores the result. On subsequent accesses the computation isn't repeated. It can only be used with val.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.code:
val a = "Kotlin"
val b = StringBuilder("Kot").append("lin").toString()
println(a == b)
println(a === b)
nezeri.exp: == compares the content (equals) — since both strings are "Kotlin", it's true. === checks the reference; since StringBuilder creates a new object, it's false.

nezeri.q: val siyahi = mutableListOf(1); siyahi.add(2) — does this work?
opts: Yes — val fixes the reference, not the object's content
nezeri.exp: val only forbids reassigning the reference. If the object itself is mutable (MutableList), its content can be changed.

nezeri.q: What does the expression 'K'.code return?
nezeri.exp: Char.code returns the character's Unicode code point as an Int. For the reverse conversion, 75.toChar() is used.

nezeri.q: What is the maximum value of the Int type?
nezeri.exp: Int is 32 bits: −2,147,483,648 … 2,147,483,647. For larger values, Long (64 bits) is used.

nezeri.q: What is the result of the expression Int.MAX_VALUE + 1?
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, integer overflow happens silently — the value wraps around to the start of the range. No error is thrown, so you need to use Long for large calculations.

nezeri.q: What is Unit in Kotlin?
opts: The counterpart of Java's void — it's a real type and has a single instance
nezeri.exp: Unit is the return type of functions that return nothing. The difference from void: Unit is a real type, can be used in generics, and only one instance of it exists.

nezeri.q: When is the Nothing type used?
opts: For expressions that never return (throw, an infinite loop)
nezeri.exp: Nothing is a type that has no values. The type of a throw expression is Nothing, which is why the construct val x = y ?: throw Xeta() works — Nothing is a subtype of all types.

nezeri.q: What is the type of x in this code?
nezeri.exp: The value is larger than the Int range (2,147,483,647), so the compiler automatically picks Long. Writing the L suffix isn't mandatory.

nezeri.q: Does Kotlin have primitive types?
opts: Yes, int and Integer are separate
No — the language only has Int, and the compiler turns it into a primitive when needed
Everything is an object and is never optimized
nezeri.exp: At the Kotlin level everything is an object, but on the JVM the compiler stores Int as a primitive int wherever possible. When it's nullable (Int?), boxing happens.

nezeri.q: val x: Int? = null; val y = x?.plus(1) — what is the type of y?
nezeri.exp: The result of a safe call (?.) is always nullable, because if the receiver is null, the result is null too. That's why the type of y is Int?.

nezeri.q: Does Kotlin have a ternary operator (condition ? a : b)?
opts: No — the if expression replaces it
nezeri.exp: Kotlin has no ternary operator, because if itself returns a value: val maks = if (a > b) a else b. This form is more readable.

nezeri.q: Is else mandatory in an if used as an expression?
nezeri.exp: An expression must always return a value. Without else, it would be unknown which value to return when the condition is false — that's why the compiler requires else.

nezeri.q: What is when the counterpart of?
nezeri.exp: when is similar to switch, but it accepts any type, ranges, type checks, and arbitrary conditions. It can also return a value.

nezeri.q: How can you group several values into the same branch in when?
nezeri.exp: The values are listed with commas: 1, 2, 3 -> "kiçik". There's no need to write consecutive cases like in Java.

nezeri.q: What does this code print?
nezeri.exp: The condition 5 > 3 is true, so the if branch runs and "boyuk" is printed.

nezeri.q: Which keyword is used in when for "all remaining cases"?
nezeri.exp: Kotlin uses else. It's mandatory in a when used as an expression — but with enum and sealed types it isn't needed if all cases are covered.

nezeri.q: Which value is returned in an if expression with a block?
nezeri.exp: The last expression of the block becomes the result. That's why there's no need to write a separate return in if blocks.

nezeri.q: Which operator is used to write the "and" operation in a condition?
nezeri.exp: For logical "and", && is used, and short-circuit evaluation applies — if the left side is false, the right side isn't evaluated at all.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: 85 >= 90 is false, 85 >= 70 is true — so "Yaxsi" is chosen and assigned to the q variable.

nezeri.q: How do you write a range check in when?
nezeri.exp: With the in keyword: in 1..10 -> "kicik". For the opposite, !in is used.

nezeri.q: When is a when without an argument useful?
opts: For checking conditions that don't depend on each other — it replaces an if-else chain
nezeri.exp: In the form when { a > 10 -> ...; b.isEmpty() -> ... }, each branch is an independent Boolean condition. This makes long if-else if chains more readable.

nezeri.q: Does a smart cast happen when you use is inside when?
opts: No, you have to cast manually
Yes — inside the branch the object is automatically seen as a String
nezeri.exp: After an is check, the compiler sees the variable as that type. There's no need to write an extra (obyekt as String).

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: The value 6 doesn't fall into the range of the first branch (1..5), but it's listed explicitly in the second branch — so "istirahet" is chosen.

nezeri.q: What does the construct when (val n = hesabla()) { ... } do?
opts: It stores the result in a variable and uses it inside that when
nezeri.exp: You can declare a variable in the subject of when. The function is called only once, and the result is available in all branches.

nezeri.q: When is else NOT needed in a when used with an enum?
opts: If all enum constants are covered
Only when there are two constants
nezeri.exp: The compiler knows all the values of the enum. If all of them are listed, the when is considered exhaustive and else isn't required.

nezeri.q: What does short-circuiting mean for the && operator?
opts: If the left side is false, the right side isn't evaluated
The right side is evaluated first
nezeri.exp: If the left side determines the result, the right side isn't executed. This makes checks like siyahi != null && siyahi.isNotEmpty() safe.

nezeri.q: Can you return an if expression directly from a function?
nezeri.code: fun boyuk(a: Int, b: Int) = if (a > b) a else b
opts: Yes — in the single-expression function form
nezeri.exp: Since if returns a value, it can be the body of a single-expression function. This is a commonly used idiomatic form.

nezeri.q: What's the advantage of when with a sealed class?
opts: Since all subclasses are known, else isn't needed, and the compiler warns you when you add a new subclass
nezeri.exp: All subclasses of a sealed hierarchy are known to the compiler. When you add a new subclass, every when block that doesn't handle it gives a compilation error — no case is forgotten.

nezeri.q: Is this when exhaustive?
opts: Yes — all enum values are covered
nezeri.exp: Both enum constants are listed, so the when is exhaustive and else isn't required.

nezeri.q: In what order are the branches in when checked?
opts: Top to bottom, the first match runs
nezeri.exp: The branches are checked in the order they're written, and the first match is executed. That's why more specific conditions should be written higher up.

nezeri.q: Can you put the result of an if directly into a string template?
nezeri.exp: Any expression can be written inside ${...}, including if. But for readability, it's better to extract complex logic into a separate variable.

nezeri.q: Why is it bad to check a Boolean value with if and return true/false?
nezeri.code: if (x > 5) true else false
opts: It's unnecessary — x > 5 already returns a Boolean by itself
nezeri.exp: The result of a comparison is already a Boolean. Just writing x > 5 is enough — this is considered a common code smell.

nezeri.q: If all the branches of a when return different types, what is the type of the result?
opts: The closest common supertype (in this case Any?)
nezeri.exp: The compiler picks the common supertype of all branches. For String, Int and null, that's Any?. It's recommended to avoid such cases and keep the type uniform.

nezeri.q: Which approach is recommended instead of many nested ifs?
opts: An early return or a when without an argument
nezeri.exp: An early return (val x = giris ?: return) and a when without an argument flatten the code. Deeply nested conditions create a "pyramid" and reduce readability.

nezeri.q: Does Kotlin have the classic for (i = 0; i < n; i++) form?
opts: No — ranges and iterator-based for are used
nezeri.exp: Kotlin has no C-style for. Instead, the for (i in 0 until n) or for (element in kolleksiya) forms are used — they're shorter and less error-prone.

nezeri.q: Which numbers does the range 1..5 include?
nezeri.exp: The .. operator includes both ends (a closed range). To exclude the last number, ..< or until is used.

nezeri.q: How many numbers does the range 0..<5 give?
nezeri.exp: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — that is, 5 numbers. ..< doesn't include the last number (it used to be called until).

nezeri.q: Which keyword is used for a descending range?
nezeri.exp: 10 downTo 1 creates a descending sequence. If you just write 10..1, the range is empty and the loop doesn't run at all.

nezeri.q: Which keyword is used to change the step?
nezeri.exp: 1..10 step 2 → 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. step must always be positive; for counting down it's used together with downTo.

nezeri.q: What's the difference between while and do-while?
opts: do-while runs the body at least once
nezeri.exp: while checks the condition at the start — if the condition is false, the body doesn't run at all. do-while runs the body and then checks the condition, so it executes at least once.

nezeri.q: What does break do?
nezeri.exp: break stops the loop immediately, and execution continues from the line after the loop. To skip only the current step, continue is used.

nezeri.q: What does continue do?
opts: Skips the current step and moves on to the next one
nezeri.exp: continue skips the rest of the body and moves on to the next iteration. The loop keeps going.

nezeri.q: What does this code print?
nezeri.exp: The range 1..3 includes both ends: 1, 2, 3. Since print() doesn't change the line, they all come out on one line.

nezeri.q: What is used to iterate over a collection together with its index?
nezeri.exp: In the form for ((index, deyer) in siyahi.withIndex()), you get both the index and the value. If you only need the indices, siyahi.indices is used.

nezeri.q: What does repeat(3) { ... } do?
nezeri.exp: repeat() is an inline function from the standard library. It simply runs the block n times and passes the iteration index as the lambda parameter.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: It starts at 10 and decreases by 3 each time: 10, 7, 4, 1. The next value (−2) falls outside the range.

nezeri.q: How do you write a for over a Map?
nezeri.exp: The elements of a Map are Entry objects and support destructuring, so you can write for ((acar, deyer) in map).

nezeri.q: What does a plain return inside forEach do?
nezeri.exp: Since forEach is inline, return exits the outer function (a non-local return). To skip only the step, you need to write return@forEach.

nezeri.q: What is used to exit nested loops all at once?
nezeri.exp: The loop is given a label (xarici@ for ...) and you write break@xarici. A break without a label exits only the innermost loop.

nezeri.q: What does (1..10).sum() return?
nezeri.exp: The sum of the numbers from 1 to 10: 10 × 11 / 2 = 55. Ranges support collection functions.

nezeri.q: How many times does this code run?
nezeri.exp: The condition is checked at the start: 0 > 5 is false, so the body doesn't run at all. If it were a do-while, it would run once.

nezeri.q: Can you write a Char range?
nezeri.code: for (c in 'a'..'e') print(c)
nezeri.exp: Since Char is also Comparable, you can create a range of it. It iterates over characters whose Unicode codes are consecutive.

nezeri.q: Does a range (IntRange) create an object, or is it optimized away?
opts: In a for loop the compiler turns it into a plain counter — no object is created
nezeri.exp: In the for (i in 1..n) construct, the compiler doesn't create an IntRange object — it turns it into a plain indexed loop. But if you store the range in a variable, an object is created.

nezeri.q: What does return@forEach do?
opts: Exits only the current lambda call — it works like continue
nezeri.exp: A labeled return exits only the lambda, which means it skips that step. The outer function keeps running.

nezeri.q: What does this code print?
nezeri.exp: On each outer step j=1 is printed; when j=2, continue@xarici leaves the inner loop and moves on to the next i. Result: 11, 21, 31.

nezeri.q: What is the idiomatic way to write an infinite loop?
nezeri.exp: while (true) is the clearest form. Kotlin has no for (;;) syntax. Such loops must always be exited with break or return.

nezeri.q: What is recommended for chained operations on a large collection?
opts: asSequence() — no intermediate lists are created
nezeri.exp: In a regular chain, each step creates a new list. A Sequence processes the elements one by one and doesn't create intermediate collections — with large data this saves a lot.

nezeri.q: What does the indices property return?
nezeri.exp: siyahi.indices → IntRange. It's used to iterate over indices in the form for (i in siyahi.indices). For the last index there's lastIndex.

nezeri.q: How many elements does this loop print?
nezeri.exp: indices → 0..4, and with step 2 the indices 0, 2, 4 are selected — so 3 elements (1, 3, 5) are printed.

nezeri.q: What is the difference between String and String?
opts: String? can hold null, String can't
nezeri.exp: The question mark at the end means the type is nullable. Assigning null to a variable of type String is a compile error — this prevents NPEs.

nezeri.q: Which one is the safe call operator?
nezeri.exp: The ?. operator skips the call entirely when the receiver is null, and the result is null. No crash happens.

nezeri.q: In the expression ad?.length, what is the result if ad is null?
nezeri.exp: A safe call returns null for a null receiver. If you need a fallback value, add the elvis operator: ad?.length ?: 0.

nezeri.q: What does the Elvis operator (?:) do?
opts: Returns the value on the right when the left side is null
Checks for null and throws an error
nezeri.exp: ad ?: "Qonaq" — returns ad if it isn't null, and "Qonaq" if it is. It got its name because it looks like Elvis Presley's hairstyle.

nezeri.q: What does the !! operator do?
opts: Forces a nullable value to non-null, throws an NPE if it is null
nezeri.exp: !! is the «not-null assertion». If you're wrong, you get a NullPointerException. Every !! in your code is a potential crash point.

nezeri.q: Which approach is safer?
nezeri.exp: A safe call combined with elvis never crashes — in the null case it returns the fallback value you defined. !!, on the other hand, can crash at runtime.

nezeri.q: What does isNullOrEmpty() check?
opts: Whether the length is greater than 1
nezeri.exp: Returns true if the variable is null OR empty. If you also need to catch text made only of whitespace, use isNullOrBlank().

nezeri.q: What does the orEmpty() function do?
opts: Returns an empty string or an empty collection when the value is null
nezeri.exp: It turns a nullable collection or string into a safe form: siyahi.orEmpty() returns an empty list if it's null, so the operations that follow are safe.

nezeri.q: What does this code print?
nezeri.exp: Since ad is null, the elvis operator returns the value on the right, "Qonaq".

nezeri.q: What is a smart cast?
opts: The compiler automatically treating a variable as non-null after a null check
nezeri.exp: Inside an if (ad != null) block the compiler sees ad as a String — no need to write ?. anymore. The same thing happens after an is check.

nezeri.q: In which case does smart cast NOT work?
opts: With var class properties — another thread could change them
There's no case where it doesn't work
nezeri.exp: A mutable class property can change between the check and its use, so the compiler can't guarantee anything. The fix: copy the value into a local val.

nezeri.q: What does the as? operator do?
opts: Returns null if the cast isn't possible
nezeri.exp: It's a safe cast: if it fails, it returns null instead of throwing ClassCastException. It's usually used together with elvis: x as? String ?: "defolt".

nezeri.q: When does the ?.let { } construct run?
opts: Only when the receiver is NOT null
Only when the receiver is null
nezeri.exp: The safe call invokes let only when the value exists. Inside the block, it is already of a non-null type.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: Since s isn't null, the safe call returns the length value (6) and the right side of the elvis operator never runs.

nezeri.q: What is lateinit for?
opts: To assign a non-null variable later — without writing null checks
nezeri.exp: In cases like dependency injection or onCreate(), the value arrives later, but logically it's never null. lateinit saves you from writing ?. on every access.

nezeri.q: What happens if a lateinit variable is used before it's assigned?
nezeri.exp: A special exception is thrown at runtime. You can check whether it has been assigned with ::xasse.isInitialized.

nezeri.q: What does filterNotNull() do?
opts: Drops null elements from the collection and makes the type non-null
nezeri.exp: It turns a List<String?> into a List<String>, dropping the nulls along the way — ideal for the operations that follow.

nezeri.q: How do you write an early exit with the elvis operator?
nezeri.exp: Since the type of a return expression is Nothing, it can stand on the right side of elvis. This is a very common idiomatic form.

nezeri.q: How do types coming from Java look in Kotlin?
opts: Platform type (String!) — the compiler doesn't check them
nezeri.exp: Java has no information about null. Kotlin shows such types as String! and doesn't check them — so an NPE is still possible. If the Java side has @Nullable/@NotNull annotations, Kotlin respects them.

nezeri.q: What is the difference between requireNotNull() and checkNotNull()?
opts: require throws IllegalArgumentException, check throws IllegalStateException
check is used only in tests
nezeri.exp: require is for validating arguments (the input is wrong), while check is for the object's state (internal logic is broken). The exception type thrown is chosen accordingly.

nezeri.q: val x: Int? = null; val y = x?.plus(1) — what is the type of y?
nezeri.exp: The result of a safe call is always nullable, because if the receiver is null, the result is null too.

nezeri.q: Can you write an extension function for a nullable type?
nezeri.code: fun String?.bosdurmu() = this == null || isEmpty()
opts: Yes — the receiver can be null and is checked inside
nezeri.exp: When the receiver is declared nullable, you can call the function without ?. Inside, this can be null, so checking it is the function's own responsibility. isNullOrEmpty() is written exactly this way.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: filterNotNull() drops the null element, leaving "a" and "b" — that is, 2 elements.

nezeri.q: What does mapNotNull { } do?
opts: Transforms and drops elements whose result is null
nezeri.exp: It's a combination of map and filterNotNull. When the transform function returns null, the element doesn't make it into the result — very handy for parsing.

nezeri.q: When is it acceptable to use the !! operator in Kotlin?
opts: Almost never; only if something outside the code guarantees it isn't null
nezeri.exp: Every !! is a potential crash. When you see one in code, ask: why can't this value be null? If you have an answer, make the type non-null from the start; if not, use ?. or ?:.

nezeri.q: What kind of collection does listOf() return?
nezeri.exp: listOf() returns the List interface — it has no add() or remove() methods. If you need to modify it, use mutableListOf().

nezeri.q: What is the main difference between a Set and a List?
opts: A Set doesn't keep duplicate elements
nezeri.exp: A Set holds unique elements — the same value isn't added a second time. A List, on the other hand, allows duplicates and preserves order.

nezeri.q: What is a Map?
nezeri.exp: A Map binds each key to a value. Keys are unique; you create one like mapOf("ad" to "Aysel").

nezeri.q: What does the map { } function do?
opts: Transforms each element and returns a new list
nezeri.exp: map() applies a transformation to each element and builds a new list from the results. The original collection doesn't change.

nezeri.q: What does the filter { } function do?
opts: Keeps the elements that match the condition
nezeri.exp: filter() selects the elements for which the predicate returns true. To get the opposite, use filterNot().

nezeri.q: How do you find out the number of elements in a collection?
nezeri.exp: Collections have a size property. String uses length instead — the two are often mixed up. There's also a count() function, which can work with a condition.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: map() multiplies each element by two: 1→2, 2→4, 3→6.

nezeri.q: What do you use to safely get the first element of a list?
nezeri.exp: first() throws NoSuchElementException on an empty collection. firstOrNull() returns null instead — it's safer.

nezeri.q: What does the sum() function return?
nezeri.exp: sum() calculates the sum of a collection of numbers. To sum over objects, use sumOf { it.qiymet }.

nezeri.q: Is a «read-only» List really immutable?
opts: No — if the underlying object is a MutableList and a reference to it remains, it can change
nezeri.exp: The List interface doesn't offer modification methods, but it doesn't guarantee full immutability. For a real copy, use toList().

nezeri.q: What does groupBy { } return?
opts: Map — the key comes from the selector, the value is a list of elements
nezeri.exp: groupBy() groups elements by key and returns a Map<K, List<T>>. For example, to group employees by department.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: First, filter selects the even numbers → [2, 4]. Then map takes the square of each → [4, 16].

nezeri.q: What is the difference between fold() and reduce()?
opts: fold takes an initial value, while reduce starts from the first element
nezeri.exp: With fold(0) { akk, x -> ... } you provide the initial value yourself — it works on an empty collection too. reduce takes the first element as the starting point and throws an exception on an empty collection.

nezeri.q: What do any { } and all { } return?
opts: Boolean — whether at least one / all of them satisfy the condition
nezeri.exp: any() returns true if at least one element satisfies the condition, and all() returns true if every element does. none() checks the opposite.

nezeri.q: What does flatten() do?
opts: Flattens nested collections into a single level
nezeri.exp: listOf(listOf(1,2), listOf(3)) → [1, 2, 3]. If you need both transforming and flattening, use flatMap { }.

nezeri.q: What does the zip() function do?
nezeri.exp: listOf(1,2).zip(listOf("a","b")) → [(1, a), (2, b)]. If the lengths differ, you get as many pairs as the shorter one's length.

nezeri.q: What does partition { } return?
opts: A Pair of two lists — matching and non-matching
nezeri.exp: val (cutler, tekler) = r.partition { it % 2 == 0 } — splits the collection into two parts in a single pass.

nezeri.q: What does distinct() do?
nezeri.exp: It keeps the first occurrence and doesn't break the order. To deduplicate by a key, there's distinctBy { }.

nezeri.q: What does associateWith { } return?
opts: Map — the elements become keys, the lambda result becomes the value
nezeri.exp: listOf("a","bb").associateWith { it.length } → {a=1, bb=2}. For the reverse, use associateBy { } — there the lambda provides the key.

nezeri.q: When is a Sequence better than a List?
opts: In a multi-step chain on a large collection — no intermediate lists are created
nezeri.exp: In a regular chain, each step creates a new list. A Sequence is lazy and processes elements one by one. With small collections, though, it can be slower because of its own overhead.

nezeri.q: When does computation start in a Sequence?
opts: When a terminal operation (toList, sum, first) is called
nezeri.exp: Intermediate operations like map and filter only build a plan. Computation starts when a terminal operation such as toList(), sum() or first() is called.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: groupBy groups by the first letter: the ones starting with a go into one list, the one starting with b into a separate one. The result is a Map<Char, List<String>>.

nezeri.q: What does chunked(2) do?
opts: Splits the collection into chunks of 2 elements
nezeri.exp: listOf(1,2,3,4,5).chunked(2) → [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]. The last chunk can be incomplete. For a sliding window, there's windowed().

nezeri.q: What is the difference between sumOf { } and sum()?
nezeri.exp: sum() works directly on collections of numbers. sumOf { it.qiymet } extracts a field from objects and sums it — it replaces the map { }.sum() chain.

nezeri.q: Why is it useful to convert a MutableList to a List?
opts: To prevent it from being modified from outside when returning it from an API
nezeri.exp: If you copy the internal mutable list with toList() and return that, the caller can't modify it. Just declaring the type as List isn't enough — the underlying object still stays mutable.

nezeri.q: Which keyword is used to declare a function?
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, a function is declared with the fun keyword: fun ad(parametrler): QaytarmaTipi { }

nezeri.q: Where is the return type written?
opts: After the parameters, with a colon
nezeri.exp: fun topla(a: Int, b: Int): Int { } — the type comes after the parameter list. This differs from Java, where the type is written before the name.

nezeri.q: What is the type of a function that returns nothing?
nezeri.exp: Unit is the counterpart of Java's void. Writing it is optional — the compiler adds it on its own.

nezeri.q: How do you write a single-expression function?
nezeri.exp: With an equals sign: fun kvadrat(x: Int) = x * x. No need for curly braces or return, and the return type is inferred too.

nezeri.q: What is a default parameter value for?
opts: A value used when no argument is passed — no need to write overloads
nezeri.exp: fun salamla(ad: String = "Dunya") — in a call without arguments, the default value is used. This replaces dozens of overload variants in Java.

nezeri.q: What is a named argument?
opts: Explicitly writing the parameter name in the call: salamla(ad = "Aysel")
nezeri.exp: Named arguments make a call readable and let you skip parameters in the middle. They're especially important for Boolean parameters.

nezeri.q: What does vararg do?
opts: Lets you pass any number of arguments to a function
nezeri.exp: fun cemle(vararg r: Int) — both cemle(1, 2, 3) and cemle(1) work. Inside, the parameter looks like an array.

nezeri.q: What does this function return?
nezeri.code: fun salamla(ad: String) = "Salam, $ad!"
nezeri.exp: In a single-expression function, the return type is inferred from the expression. Since a string template gives a String, the function's type is String.

nezeri.q: Does a function have to be inside a class?
opts: No — it can be declared directly in a file (top-level)
nezeri.exp: This is an important difference between Kotlin and Java. There's no need to wrap helper functions in a class — on the JVM they become static methods of a FaylAdiKt class.

nezeri.q: How do you pass an existing array to a vararg parameter?
nezeri.exp: The asterisk (*) is the spread operator — it unpacks the array into separate arguments. Without it, the array is passed as a single argument and you get a type mismatch.

nezeri.q: What is a local function?
opts: A function declared inside another function
nezeri.exp: A local function is visible only inside its enclosing function and has access to the outer variables. It's handy for extracting repeated helper logic.

nezeri.q: Which one is NOT a requirement for an infix function?
opts: It must be a member or extension function
It must take a single parameter
The parameter must not have a default value
nezeri.exp: There's no restriction on the return type. The other three requirements are mandatory, though. Example: 1 to "bir" — to is an infix function from the standard library.

nezeri.q: What does tailrec do?
opts: Turns tail recursion into a loop — prevents StackOverflow
nezeri.exp: When the recursive call is the LAST operation of the function, the compiler turns it into a regular loop. Then the stack doesn't overflow even a million levels deep.

nezeri.q: Can this function be tailrec?
nezeri.code:
fun faktorial(n: Int): Int =
    if (n <= 1) 1 else n * faktorial(n - 1)
opts: No — there's a multiplication after the recursive call
nezeri.exp: For tail recursion, the recursive call must be the last operation. Here the result is multiplied by n after it returns, so tailrec doesn't work — you need to add an accumulator parameter.

nezeri.q: Can you overload functions in Kotlin?
opts: Yes — functions with the same name and different parameter signatures
nezeri.exp: Overloading is possible, but default parameters are often the better solution — they give you less code and a clearer API.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: Thanks to the named argument, you can skip the parameter in the middle and change only sonluq. ad keeps its default value.

nezeri.q: Are function parameters val or var?
opts: val — they can't be changed inside the function
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, parameters are always read-only. If you need to change the value, you have to create a local variable.

nezeri.q: What does a function returning Nothing mean?
opts: It never returns normally — it throws an exception or runs forever
nezeri.exp: Unit returns but carries no meaningful value; Nothing never returns at all. The TODO() and error() functions return Nothing, which is why they can be used on the right side of elvis.

nezeri.q: What do you need to call a Kotlin function with default parameters from Java?
nezeri.exp: Java doesn't know about default parameters. @JvmOverloads tells the compiler to generate a separate overload for each parameter combination.

nezeri.q: What number does this code print?
nezeri.exp: A local function gets access to the enclosing function's variables and can modify them (closure). Two calls bring the counter to 2.

nezeri.q: If an extension function and a member method have the same signature, which one runs?
opts: The member method always takes precedence
nezeri.exp: The member method always wins. So if you write an extension with the same name for an existing class, it will never be called — a source of silent bugs.

nezeri.q: Is this function a correct tailrec?
nezeri.code:
tailrec fun cemle(n: Int, akk: Int = 0): Int =
    if (n == 0) akk else cemle(n - 1, akk + n)
opts: Yes — the recursive call is the last operation
nezeri.exp: Thanks to the accumulator, the result isn't modified after the call — the recursive call really is the last operation. The compiler turns it into a loop.

nezeri.q: How do top-level functions look in Java?
opts: As static methods of a FaylAdiKt class
nezeri.exp: Functions in the Komekciler.kt file become static methods of the KomekcilerKt class in Java. To change the name, use @file:JvmName.

nezeri.q: How do you write the type to pass a function as a function parameter?
nezeri.exp: A function type has the form (parameters) -> return. For a function with no parameters and no result, you write () -> Unit.

nezeri.q: Why is a default parameter useful in a recursive function?
opts: It hides the accumulator — the caller doesn't need to know about it
nezeri.exp: Writing cemle(100) is enough; the accumulator's initial value (0) is set by default. This hides an internal detail from the API.

nezeri.q: What is a lambda?
nezeri.exp: A lambda is an anonymous function: { a, b -> a + b }. It can be stored in a variable, passed as a parameter and returned.

nezeri.q: Which brackets is a lambda written in?
nezeri.exp: A lambda is written inside curly braces. The parameters come before the arrow (->): { x -> x * 2 }.

nezeri.q: What is the default parameter name in a single-parameter lambda?
nezeri.exp: If you don't write a parameter name, Kotlin automatically names it it: list.map { it * 2 }. This is the most commonly used form.

nezeri.q: What is a higher-order function (HOF)?
opts: A function that takes a function or returns a function
nezeri.exp: map, filter, forEach — they're all HOFs, because they take a function as a parameter. Functions that return functions also count as HOFs.

nezeri.q: How is a lambda's result returned?
opts: The last line automatically becomes the result
nezeri.exp: You don't write return inside a lambda — the last expression is the result. An explicit return is only possible with a label: return@map.

nezeri.q: What does the type (Int) -> String mean?
opts: A function that takes an Int and returns a String
nezeri.exp: The parameter types are written before the arrow, and the return type after it. A function with no parameters and no result: () -> Unit.

nezeri.q: What does this code print?
nezeri.exp: The lambda is stored in a variable and called like a regular function: 21 * 2 = 42.

nezeri.q: What is a trailing lambda?
opts: Moving the last lambda outside the parentheses
nezeri.exp: If a lambda is the last parameter, it can be moved outside the parentheses: list.filter { it > 1 }. This is the foundation of Kotlin DSLs.

nezeri.q: What does forEach do?
opts: Performs an operation on each element and returns no result
nezeri.exp: forEach returns Unit — it's only for side effects (printing, logging). If you need a transformation, use map.

nezeri.q: How do you write a function reference?
nezeri.exp: With a double colon: list.filter(::ciftdir). It's a shorthand for writing { ciftdir(it) }. A method reference: String::uppercase.

nezeri.q: What does the inline keyword do?
opts: Copies the function's body to the call site — no lambda object is created
nezeri.exp: Every lambda is actually an object. inline tells the compiler to expand the body directly at the call site, which removes the cost of creating an object.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: filter selects the ones greater than 2 → [3, 4], then map multiplies each by 10 → [30, 40].

nezeri.q: What is a closure?
opts: A lambda's ability to capture and use variables from the outer scope
nezeri.exp: Unlike Java, Kotlin lambdas can both read and MODIFY a captured variable — there's no requirement for it to be final.

nezeri.q: How is an anonymous function different from a lambda?
opts: In an anonymous function the return type can be written explicitly, and return exits the function itself
nezeri.exp: val bol = fun(a: Int, b: Int): Int { if (b == 0) return 0; return a / b } — here return exits only the anonymous function. That isn't possible in a lambda.

nezeri.q: What is noinline for?
opts: To allow a particular lambda in an inline function to be kept as an object
nezeri.exp: An inlined lambda can't be stored in a variable. If you need to pass it somewhere else or store it, mark it with noinline.

nezeri.q: What does crossinline do?
opts: Forbids returning from the outer function inside the lambda
nezeri.exp: If the lambda will be called in another context (for example inside a Thread), a non-local return becomes dangerous. crossinline forbids it.

nezeri.q: How do you write a function that returns a function?
nezeri.code: fun vurucu(k: Int): (Int) -> Int = { it * k }
opts: The return type is a function type and a lambda is returned
nezeri.exp: Function types can be used just like regular types. The call vurucu(3) returns an (Int) -> Int, which you can then call: vurucu(3)(7) → 21.

nezeri.q: Out of several parameters, which lambda can be moved outside the parentheses?
nezeri.exp: Only the LAST parameter can be a trailing lambda. fold(0) { akk, x -> akk + x } — the initial value goes in the parentheses, the lambda outside.

nezeri.q: What is reified needed for?
opts: To see a generic type at runtime in an inline function
nezeri.exp: On the JVM, generic types are erased (type erasure). inline + reified lets the compiler write the type into the call site, which makes an x is T check possible.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: The lambda captures the say variable (closure) and can modify it. After two calls, the value becomes 2.

nezeri.q: What does a plain return inside forEach do?
nezeri.exp: Since forEach is inline, return exits the outer function. To just skip a step, you need to write return@forEach.

nezeri.q: Are the map, filter and let functions in the standard library inline?
opts: Yes — no lambda object is created
nezeri.exp: All of these small HOFs are declared inline. That's why chained operations run without the extra cost of creating objects.

nezeri.q: When is it NOT RIGHT to use inline?
opts: In small functions that take a lambda
In functions with a large body — the bytecode bloats
nezeri.exp: inline copies the body to every call site. In a large function, this bloats the bytecode and does more harm than good. In a function that doesn't take a lambda, it's pointless altogether.

nezeri.q: What is the expression String::uppercase?
opts: A method reference — the same as { it.uppercase() }
nezeri.exp: It's an unbound method reference: the receiver is passed as a parameter. It's used in the form list.map(String::uppercase).

nezeri.q: If the last expression of a lambda is Unit, what is the result?
nezeri.code: val f: (Int) -> Unit = { println(it) }
nezeri.exp: If the function type requires Unit, the value of the last expression is discarded and Unit is returned. This is normal in functions like forEach.

nezeri.q: How many main scope functions are there in Kotlin?
nezeri.exp: Five: let, run, with, apply, also. They differ in only two things — how you refer to the object (it/this) and what is returned.

nezeri.q: How do you refer to the context object inside let?
nezeri.exp: let and also use it; run, with and apply use this. You can replace it with your own name: let { istifadeci -> ... }

nezeri.q: What does apply return?
nezeri.exp: apply and also return the receiver object itself. That's why they don't break the chain and are ideal for building objects.

nezeri.q: What does let return?
opts: The last expression of the lambda
nezeri.exp: let, run and with return the lambda result. That's why they're used for transformations.

nezeri.q: Which scope function is best for a null check?
nezeri.exp: The ad?.let { } block runs only when the value isn't null, and inside it it is already a non-null type.

nezeri.q: Which function is used to build an object (builder style)?
nezeri.exp: Inside apply you use this, so you can set properties directly: Istifadeci().apply { ad = "Aysel" }. At the end, the object itself is returned.

nezeri.q: What is also mainly used for?
nezeri.exp: Since also returns the object itself, it doesn't break the chain. Using it makes it more readable for logging.

nezeri.q: How does with differ from the others?
opts: It isn't an extension function — the object is passed as an argument
nezeri.exp: It has the form with(obyekt) { }, not obyekt.with { }. That's why it can't be used directly with a nullable object.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: let returns the lambda result. it.length is 6, and that is assigned to the variable n.

nezeri.q: What is the main difference between apply and also?
opts: apply returns the object, also returns the result
Both return the object — the only difference is the this/it context
nezeri.exp: Both return the receiver. Inside apply you get this (you can set properties directly), inside also you get it (clearer for side effects).

nezeri.q: What is the difference between run and let?
opts: run uses this, let uses it — both return a result
nezeri.exp: Functionally they're the same. The choice is a matter of style: use run if you access the object's members a lot, and let if you want to bind the value to another name.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: Inside apply, this = the A object, so x = 5 changes the object's property directly. At the end, the object itself is returned.

nezeri.q: What does takeIf return?
opts: The object if the condition holds, otherwise null
nezeri.exp: "".takeIf { it.isNotBlank() } → null. It's handy for producing a null conditionally and combining it with elvis.

nezeri.q: What does takeUnless do?
opts: It returns the object if the condition does NOT hold
nezeri.exp: It's the opposite of takeIf. x.takeUnless { it.isEmpty() } returns the object if it's NOT empty.

nezeri.q: Can you use with on a nullable object?
opts: Not directly — since with isn't an extension function, ?. can't be applied
nezeri.exp: In the with(obyekt) form there's no place to put ?. For nullable values you use obyekt?.let { } or obyekt?.run { }.

nezeri.q: What does this code print?
nezeri.exp: also first prints the current state ([1, 2]), then apply adds an element. Since both return the object itself, the chain continues.

nezeri.q: Can you rename it inside a let block?
nezeri.exp: You can give the lambda parameter your own name. In nested let blocks this greatly improves readability.

nezeri.q: Which case is run best suited for?
opts: Configuring an object and computing a result
nezeri.exp: run gives you the this context (direct access to members) and also returns a result. It's ideal for combining configuration + computation.

nezeri.q: Why is heavy nesting of scope functions bad?
opts: this and it get mixed up, and the code becomes unreadable
nezeri.exp: With more than two levels of nested blocks, it gets hard to track which this refers to which object. In such cases, a plain variable and if are better.

nezeri.q: Which function was chosen incorrectly in this code?
nezeri.code: val uzunluq = ad.apply { length }
opts: apply — it returns the object itself, so you don't get the length; you need let or run
nezeri.exp: apply returns the receiver, so the uzunluq variable becomes a String, not an Int. If you need a result, use run or let.

nezeri.q: Are scope functions inline?
opts: Yes — no lambda object is created, so there's no performance overhead
nezeri.exp: All of them are declared inline. That's why using them adds no extra runtime overhead compared to plain code.

nezeri.q: What is the main advantage of also in a chain?
opts: It lets you insert a side effect (log, check) without breaking the chain
nezeri.exp: Since it returns the object itself, you can add a debug print or validation in the middle of the chain — the following operations aren't affected.

nezeri.q: What do you get when you combine takeIf and elvis?
nezeri.code: val ad = giris.takeIf { it.isNotBlank() } ?: "Qonaq"
opts: The non-empty input, or "Qonaq" if it's empty
nezeri.exp: takeIf gives null if the condition doesn't hold, and elvis catches it and returns the fallback value. This is a very readable form for validation.

nezeri.q: Inside apply, if there's a local variable and a property with the same name, which one is used?
nezeri.exp: The name in the nearest scope wins. To refer to the property explicitly you have to write this.ad — this is one of apply's hidden pitfalls.

nezeri.q: Which scope function is NOT an extension function?
nezeri.exp: with is a regular function and takes the object as an argument. The rest are extension functions, so they're called with a dot and support ?.

nezeri.q: Do you need the new keyword to create an object in Kotlin?
nezeri.exp: Kotlin has no new. An object's constructor is called like a regular function: val u = Istifadeci("Aysel").

nezeri.q: Where is the primary constructor written?
opts: Right after the class name, in parentheses
nezeri.exp: class Istifadeci(val ad: String) — the constructor is part of the class header. This is one of the features that makes Kotlin much more concise.

nezeri.q: What does writing a constructor parameter with val do?
opts: It also turns it into a class property
nezeri.exp: class A(val x: Int) — x is both a parameter and a property. Without val it's only a constructor parameter and isn't accessible in the body.

nezeri.q: When does the init block run?
nezeri.exp: The init block runs while the object is being constructed, as part of the primary constructor. There can be several init blocks — they run in the order they're written.

nezeri.q: Do you have to write getters/setters for properties by hand in Kotlin?
nezeri.exp: A getter is generated for val, and both a getter and a setter for var. You only write them by hand when you need custom behavior.

nezeri.q: What is the default visibility modifier?
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, everything is public by default. That differs from Java, where the default is package-private.

nezeri.q: What does the internal modifier mean?
nezeri.exp: internal is visible within the same compilation module (Gradle module). It's useful for hiding internal API when writing a library.

nezeri.q: How many properties does this code create?
nezeri.code: class A(val x: Int, y: Int)
nezeri.exp: Only x is a property, because it's marked with val. y is just a constructor parameter and isn't accessible outside the init block.

nezeri.q: If the class body is empty, do you need curly braces?
nezeri.exp: If the body is empty, the braces can be left out entirely. This is handy for marker classes.

nezeri.q: What must a secondary constructor do?
opts: It must delegate to the primary constructor: this(...)
nezeri.exp: If there's a primary constructor, a secondary constructor must delegate to it. Thanks to default parameters, you rarely need a secondary constructor in Kotlin.

nezeri.q: How do you refer to the backing field in a custom setter?
nezeri.exp: field is a special identifier and is only accessible inside an accessor. If you write this.xasse, you get infinite recursion.

nezeri.q: Does a computed property (custom getter) take up a field?
nezeri.code:
val tamAd: String
    get() = "$ad $soyad"
opts: No — it's recomputed on every access
nezeri.exp: A backing field is created only when the field identifier is used. Here the value is recomputed every time — if you need caching, use by lazy.

nezeri.q: What does private set do?
opts: It allows reading, but keeps writing only inside the class
nezeri.exp:
var status: String = "aktiv"
    private set — it can be read from outside but can't be changed. Ideal for state that looks immutable but is managed internally.

nezeri.q: What is the difference between a nested and an inner class?
opts: inner can access the outer class's members, nested can't
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, a class inside a class is static by default (nested). If you need a reference to the outer object, you write the inner keyword.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: The custom setter turns a negative value into 0. field writes directly to the backing field, so no recursion happens.

nezeri.q: Why is require() used in a constructor?
opts: To prevent an object from being created at all with an invalid argument
nezeri.exp: Writing require(ad.isNotBlank()) in the init block immediately stops an invalid object from being created. This is the "valid state" principle.

nezeri.q: What is the default state of class members in Kotlin?
nezeri.exp: Classes, as well as methods and properties, are final by default. To override, both the class and the member must be declared open.

nezeri.q: Why would you make a constructor private?
opts: To control object creation through a factory method
nezeri.exp: private constructor + a factory method in the companion object — this way the object can only be created in a controlled way (with caching, validation).

nezeri.q: In what order do init and the property initializations run in this code?
nezeri.exp: Property initializers and init blocks run in the order they're WRITTEN in the class body. That's why you get the order birinci, init, sonuncu.

nezeri.q: How do you refer to the outer class's this from an inner class?
nezeri.exp: You use a labeled this: this@Xarici.deyer. A plain this refers to the inner class itself.

nezeri.q: Can a property's initial value use a constructor parameter?
opts: Yes — the parameter is accessible in property initializers and the init block
nezeri.exp: Even without val, the parameter can be used in property initializers and init blocks. It just isn't accessible in methods.

nezeri.q: What is the common parent of all classes in Kotlin?
nezeri.exp: Any provides the equals(), hashCode() and toString() methods. The difference from Java's Object: it has no methods like wait() and notify().

nezeri.q: What changes when you add an annotation or modifier to a constructor?
nezeri.code: class A private constructor(val x: Int)
nezeri.exp: Usually the constructor keyword is omitted. But if you write a visibility modifier or an annotation, you have to state it explicitly.

nezeri.q: Can you declare a field directly in Kotlin?
opts: No — you only declare properties; the compiler creates a field itself when needed
nezeri.exp: Kotlin has no concept of a field at the language level. You declare a property, and the compiler allocates a backing field for it when needed.

nezeri.q: How are two instances of the same class compared by default?
nezeri.code:

println(A(1) == A(1))
opts: false — equals inherited from Any compares references
nezeri.exp: In a regular class, equals isn't overridden, so a reference comparison is made. If you need content comparison, use a data class.

nezeri.q: What are classes in Kotlin by default?
nezeri.exp: All classes are final by default. This is the "design for inheritance or prohibit it" principle built into the language.

nezeri.q: Which keyword do you write to allow inheritance?
nezeri.exp: open class Heyvan — only then can you inherit from the class. Methods and properties must also be declared open separately.

nezeri.q: What is the inheritance syntax?
nezeri.exp: You use a colon and call the parent class's constructor: class It(ad: String) : Heyvan(ad).

nezeri.q: What do you write to override a method?
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, override is a keyword, not an annotation, and it's MANDATORY. This prevents overriding by accident.

nezeri.q: What do you use to call the parent class's method?
nezeri.exp: super.metod() calls the parent class's implementation. When there are several interfaces, you use the form super<Interfeys>.metod().

nezeri.q: How do you declare an interface?
nezeri.exp: With the interface keyword. An interface can have abstract methods, methods with a default body, and abstract properties.

nezeri.q: How many interfaces can a class inherit from?
nezeri.exp: A class can inherit from ONLY ONE class, but from any number of interfaces: class Ordek : Heyvan(), Ucan, Uzen.

nezeri.q: What is an abstract method?
opts: A method without a body — subclasses must implement it
nezeri.exp: abstract fun sahe(): Double — it has no body. A class with abstract members must itself be declared abstract.

nezeri.q: Can you create an object from an abstract class?
nezeri.exp: An abstract class is incomplete — its abstract members have no implementation. An object can only be created from a subclass that completes it.

nezeri.q: Can an interface hold state?
opts: No — it can't have a backing field, only abstract or computed properties
nezeri.exp: You can write val ad: String in an interface, but you can't give it a value — it's abstract. A computed property (with get()) is possible, though.

nezeri.q: What should you do if two interfaces have a default method with the same name?
opts: Override it in the class and resolve it with super<Interfeys>.metod()
nezeri.exp: The compiler requires you to resolve the conflict. In the form override fun f() { super<A>.f(); super<B>.f() } you choose yourself which implementation runs.

nezeri.q: What does the parent class need so that a property can be overridden?
nezeri.exp: Like methods, properties are final by default. To override one, it must be declared open in the parent class.

nezeri.q: Can you override a val property as a var?
opts: Yes — a val can be overridden as a var, but not the other way around
nezeri.exp: val only requires a getter; var gives both a getter and a setter — that is, it extends the contract. Going the other way would break the contract, so it's prohibited.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: super.f() first runs the parent class's implementation ("A"), then its own code runs ("B").

nezeri.q: Which difference DOES exist between an abstract class and an interface?
opts: An abstract class has a constructor, an interface doesn't
An abstract class can't have a default method
nezeri.exp: An abstract class can hold state and have a constructor. An interface only describes a contract — it has no constructor and no backing field.

nezeri.q: What does the by keyword do at the class level?
opts: It delegates the interface implementation to another object
nezeri.exp: class Loglayan(d: Cap) : Cap by d — all Cap methods are automatically forwarded to the d object. You only need to override what you need.

nezeri.q: What is polymorphism?
opts: A variable of a parent type holding a subclass object, and the real type's method being run
nezeri.exp: val h: Heyvan = It() — when you call h.sesCixar(), the It class's implementation runs. This is dynamic (virtual) dispatch.

nezeri.q: Are extension functions polymorphic?
opts: No — they're resolved statically, chosen by the declared type
nezeri.exp: Extensions aren't added to the class; they become static functions. That's why which function runs is determined by the variable's DECLARED type.

nezeri.q: Why is an open method called in the parent class's constructor dangerous?
opts: The subclass's properties aren't initialized yet — the overridden method works with an incomplete object
nezeri.exp: The parent constructor runs before the subclass's properties. If the overridden method accesses those properties, they'll still be null or 0.

nezeri.q: Can you write a computed property in an interface?
opts: Yes — you can provide a getter, but not a backing field
nezeri.exp: A getter in an interface counts as a default implementation. A backing field, however, means state and is prohibited in an interface.

nezeri.q: Can you inherit from a sealed class in another module?
opts: No — the subclasses must be in the same module
nezeri.exp: It's exactly this restriction that lets the compiler know all the subclasses and makes when exhaustive.

nezeri.q: Why is composition considered better than inheritance?
opts: It's more flexible — it isn't tied to a class hierarchy, and behavior can be changed at runtime
nezeri.exp: Inheritance creates strong coupling, and a change in the parent class can break all subclasses. Composition (made easy in Kotlin with by) gives a less coupled and more testable design.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: Extensions are resolved statically. The variable is declared with the Ana type, so Ana.tesvir() is chosen — the real type isn't taken into account.

nezeri.q: What do you write to close an overridden member to further subclasses?
nezeri.exp: final override fun f() — after this class, the method can no longer be overridden. An overridden member stays open by default.

nezeri.q: In interface delegation, is an overridden method forwarded to the delegate?
opts: No — the overridden method replaces the delegate
nezeri.exp: If you have your own implementation, it takes precedence. The delegate only handles members that aren't overridden.

nezeri.q: Which functions does a data class generate automatically?
nezeri.exp: These five groups of functions are generated based on the properties in the primary constructor. In Java the same job takes 50+ lines.

nezeri.q: At least how many parameters must a data class's primary constructor have?
nezeri.exp: It must have at least one parameter, and all of them must be marked with val/var — otherwise there'd be no data for the generated functions to be based on.

nezeri.q: What does copy() do?
opts: It creates a new copy with some fields changed
nezeri.exp: a.copy(yas = 25) — the remaining fields are taken from the original. It's the main way to work with immutable objects.

nezeri.q: What is an enum class for?
opts: For a fixed, limited set — status, color, day
nezeri.exp: You use an enum when the possible values are known in advance and limited. It's far safer than string constants.

nezeri.q: What does the object keyword create?
opts: A singleton — an object with a single instance
nezeri.exp: object Konfiq { } — a singleton built into the language. It's thread-safe and lazy; there's no need to create a separate instance.

nezeri.q: What is companion object the counterpart of?
nezeri.exp: Members that belong to the class but don't depend on an instance are written inside the companion object: constants, factory methods.

nezeri.q: What do you use to get the name of an enum constant?
nezeri.exp: Reng.QIRMIZI.name → "QIRMIZI". For the position number there's the ordinal property (it starts at 0).

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: A data class automatically generates toString(), and it shows all the properties together with the class name.

nezeri.q: What does == give for two data class objects with the same values?
nezeri.exp: A data class generates equals() based on its properties. In a regular class, a reference comparison would be made and you'd get false.

nezeri.q: In a data class, is a property declared in the BODY included in equals?
opts: No — only properties in the primary constructor are taken into account
nezeri.exp: This is a hidden source of bugs. Two objects can be considered equal even if a property in the body differs. Fields that should affect equality must be in the primary constructor.

nezeri.q: What is the main advantage of a sealed class?
opts: All subclasses are known — when becomes exhaustive, no else needed
nezeri.exp: When you add a new subclass, every when block that doesn't handle it gives a compilation error. This guarantees that no case is forgotten.

nezeri.q: Can you add properties to enum constants?
nezeri.exp: An enum can have a constructor, and each constant passes its own value to it. Methods can be added too.

nezeri.q: What is the difference between entries and values()?
opts: entries is more modern and doesn't create a new array on every call
nezeri.exp: values() returns a new array on every call. entries, on the other hand, is an immutable list and has been the recommended form since Kotlin 1.9.

nezeri.q: How many times does the init block inside an object run?
nezeri.exp: A singleton is created lazily: it's initialized on the first access and never again.

nezeri.q: How does destructuring work in a data class?
nezeri.code: val (ad, yas) = istifadeci
opts: It works automatically thanks to the componentN() functions
nezeri.exp: A data class generates component1(), component2()... Destructuring calls exactly these functions — the order is the same as in the constructor.

nezeri.q: What is the difference between a sealed interface and a sealed class?
opts: A sealed interface is more flexible — a subtype can also belong to another hierarchy
There's no such thing as a sealed interface
nezeri.exp: A class can inherit from only one parent class, but from many interfaces. That's why a sealed interface imposes fewer restrictions.

nezeri.q: What is a value class for?
opts: For type safety — no object is created at runtime
nezeri.exp: @JvmInline value class Email(val deyer: String) — the compiler stores it as a plain String, but the type system doesn't let you mix up Email and String.

nezeri.q: When is data object used?
opts: For stateless sealed subtypes — it gives a proper toString and equals
nezeri.exp: A regular object's toString isn't readable. A data object prints a clear name, and since it's a singleton, equals works correctly too.

nezeri.q: What is an anonymous object (object : Interfeys)?
opts: The counterpart of Java's anonymous class — a one-off implementation
nezeri.exp: object : Dinleyici { override fun ... } — an object with no name, created on the spot. Handy for callbacks.

nezeri.q: What do you need to call a companion object member directly as static from Java?
nezeri.exp: Without @JvmStatic, in Java you have to write Sinif.Companion.metod(). With the annotation, Sinif.metod() becomes possible.

nezeri.q: How do you write different behavior for each constant in an enum?
opts: By overriding an abstract method in each constant's own body
nezeri.exp: You declare abstract fun emr() in the enum, and each constant implements it in its own curly braces. This is a compact form of the "state pattern".

nezeri.q: Why is writing else in a when over a sealed hierarchy bad?
opts: When a new subclass is added, the compiler won't warn you — else swallows it
nezeri.exp: The main benefit of sealed is exactly the compiler check. If you write else, a new case silently falls into the else branch and the bug stays hidden until runtime.

nezeri.q: What is out used for in a generic sealed class?

opts: To pass a Netice<It> where a Netice<Heyvan> is expected (covariance)
nezeri.exp: out T says the type is only used in output positions. This makes it possible to use stateless subtypes like Netice<Nothing> anywhere.

nezeri.q: Does a data class's copy() method create a deep copy?
opts: No — it's a shallow copy, inner objects are shared
nezeri.exp: copy() copies only the top level. The same references to inner objects remain — if they're mutable, both copies are affected.

nezeri.q: Can a String be changed in Kotlin (is it mutable)?
opts: No — every operation creates a new String
nezeri.exp: String is immutable. uppercase() or replace() don't change the original — they return a new string. If you need lots of concatenation, use StringBuilder or buildString.

nezeri.q: Which property gives you the length of a string?
nezeri.exp: String has a length property. Collections use size instead — the two are often mixed up.

nezeri.q: How do you access a character of a string?
nezeri.exp: With square brackets: s[0]. The result is of type Char. If the index is out of range, a StringIndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown.

nezeri.q: What do you use to join two strings?
opts: The + operator or a string template
nezeri.exp: Both work, but a template ("$a$b") is more readable. If you need to concatenate inside a loop, buildString is more efficient.

nezeri.q: What does uppercase() do?
opts: Returns a NEW string in uppercase
nezeri.exp: The original string doesn't change — you need to assign the result to a variable. For just the first letter, use replaceFirstChar { it.uppercase() }.

nezeri.q: What does trim() do?
nezeri.exp: It only removes whitespace at the edges; whitespace in the middle stays. For one side there's trimStart() and trimEnd().

nezeri.q: What does split(",") return?
nezeri.exp: It splits by the delimiter and returns a list. The reverse operation is joinToString().

nezeri.q: What's the difference between isEmpty() and isBlank()?
opts: isBlank() also catches a string made only of whitespace
nezeri.exp: "   ".isEmpty() is false, but "   ".isBlank() is true. When validating user input, you almost always want isBlank().

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: K-o-t-l-i-n — six characters. length is a property, not a function, so you don't write parentheses.

nezeri.q: Which indices does substring(0, 3) return?
nezeri.exp: The start is included, the end is not. "Kotlin".substring(0, 3) gives "Kot".

nezeri.q: What's the advantage of a triple-quoted (raw) string?
opts: No escape characters needed, and it can span multiple lines
nezeri.exp: It saves you from a jungle of backslashes when writing regex and JSON. To clean up the indentation, add .trimIndent() — it doesn't happen automatically.

nezeri.q: What does trimIndent() do?
opts: Removes the common minimal indentation from every line
nezeri.exp: It's used so that the indentation in your code doesn't end up in a multiline string. It's calculated from the least-indented line.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: replace() replaces all matches. The word "Kotlin" has one lowercase t, and it becomes T.

nezeri.q: What does indexOf() return if nothing is found?
nezeri.exp: If nothing is found, it returns -1. That's why you should always check the result.

nezeri.q: What does padStart(3, character) do?
opts: Adds characters to the start until the length is 3
nezeri.exp: The string "7" becomes "007". If the string is already longer than 3 characters, nothing changes. To pad at the end, there's padEnd().

nezeri.q: When do you use toIntOrNull()?
opts: When you're not sure the string is a number
nezeri.exp: toInt() throws a NumberFormatException on a failed conversion. toIntOrNull() returns null instead — it's the safe option for user input.

nezeri.q: How do you write an expression in a string template?
nezeri.exp: For a simple variable, $s is enough, but if there's a dot or an operation, you need curly braces.

nezeri.q: What does the == operator compare for strings?
nezeri.exp: An important difference from Java: in Kotlin, == compares content. For reference comparison, use ===.

nezeri.q: How do you compare strings ignoring case?
nezeri.exp: equals() accepts ignoreCase as a second parameter. Alternative: a.lowercase() == b.lowercase().

nezeri.q: Why is concatenating strings inside a loop bad?
opts: A new String object is created at every step
nezeri.exp: Because String is immutable, every concatenation creates a new object. buildString or StringBuilder work with a single object and are much faster.

nezeri.q: What does buildString { } return?
nezeri.exp: Inside, you work with a StringBuilder (append, appendLine), and at the end you get a finished String back. It's an efficient and readable form.

nezeri.q: What do you use to go through a string character by character?
nezeri.exp: String is iterable. If you need the index, use s.indices or s.withIndex().

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?

nezeri.q: How are joinToString() and split() related?
opts: They're opposites — one splits, the other joins
nezeri.exp: split gives you a list by the delimiter, joinToString turns the list back into a string. You can set the separator, prefix and postfix.

nezeri.q: What does first() do on an empty string?
nezeri.exp: On an empty collection, first() throws an exception. The safe option is firstOrNull() — it returns null.

nezeri.exp: Since both operands are Int, integer division is performed and the fractional part is dropped. For a decimal result, at least one of them must be a Double.

nezeri.q: What does the % operator do?
opts: Gives the remainder of a division

nezeri.q: In Kotlin, what does the == operator compare for objects?
nezeri.exp: An important difference from Java. For reference comparison, use three equals signs (===).

nezeri.q: Which one is the logical "and" operator?
nezeri.exp: Two ampersands are used, and short-circuiting applies — if the left side is false, the right side isn't evaluated at all.

nezeri.q: Which one is the negation operator?
nezeri.exp: The exclamation mark flips a Boolean value: !true gives false.

nezeri.q: What does the in operator check?
opts: Whether an element is in a collection or range
nezeri.exp: It's used in forms like 5 in 1..10 and "a" in siyahi. For the opposite there's !in. Under the hood, contains() is called.

nezeri.q: What does the is operator do?

nezeri.q: How do you write the increment operator?

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?

nezeri.q: What does the === operator check?
opts: That two references point to the same object
nezeri.exp: It's referential equality. With data classes, == can give true while === gives false — because the objects are separate but their content is the same.

nezeri.q: What does short-circuiting mean?
opts: As soon as the result is known, the right side isn't evaluated
nezeri.exp: siyahi != null && siyahi.isNotEmpty() — if the left side is false, the right side doesn't run, so there's no NPE risk.

nezeri.q: What does the Elvis operator (?:) do?

nezeri.q: What do you write to overload an operator?
nezeri.exp: You declare a function with a special name using the operator keyword: plus, minus, times, div, get, set, contains, invoke, compareTo, etc.

nezeri.q: Which function does the expression a + b call?
nezeri.exp: Each operator is bound to a specific function name. If a class has operator fun plus(), you can add its objects with a plus sign.

nezeri.q: Which function does the expression obyekt[i] call?

nezeri.q: Which function does the expression x in obyekt call?

nezeri.q: Which function are the comparison operators (<, >) bound to?
nezeri.exp: If you implement the Comparable interface and write compareTo(), you can compare objects with the less-than/greater-than operators.

nezeri.q: What is the expression obyekt() (calling an object like a function) based on?
nezeri.exp: When operator fun invoke() is declared, the object can be called like a function. That's exactly how lambdas work under the hood, too.

nezeri.q: What does the shl operator do?
nezeri.exp: 2 shl 3 is 16 — each shift doubles the value. In Kotlin, bitwise operators are names, not symbols: shl, shr, ushr, and, or, xor, inv.

nezeri.q: What is the result of the expression 12 and 10?

nezeri.q: What is the result of the expression 12 xor 10?

nezeri.q: When is the plusAssign operator called?

nezeri.q: What's the main risk in operator overloading?
opts: If the operator's meaning is unexpected, the code becomes unreadable
nezeri.exp: A plus sign is understood as joining or adding. If you use it to mean "delete", you'll confuse the reader. Only overload an operator when it has a natural meaning.

nezeri.q: What does the unaryMinus operator represent?
nezeri.exp: It's the unary minus sign. Its counterpart is unaryPlus. These are useful in types like vectors and money.
