nezeri.q: What is an extension function?
opts: Adding a new function to a class without inheriting from it
nezeri.exp: You can add functions even to classes whose source code you don't have access to (String, List). The class doesn't change, and no inheritance is needed.

nezeri.q: How do you refer to the receiver in an extension function?
nezeri.exp: fun String.uzunmu() = this.length > 10 — this is the object it's called on. Often you can skip this entirely: length > 10.

nezeri.q: Which one is the correct declaration of an extension function?
nezeri.exp: The type name is written before the function name, with a dot: fun Type.functionName().

nezeri.q: Can an extension property have a backing field?
opts: No — you can only write a getter
nezeri.exp: No real field is added to the class, so it can't store a value. Only a computed property is possible: val String.ilkHerf get() = first().

nezeri.q: Can an extension function access a class's private members?
nezeri.exp: An extension lives outside the class, not inside it — so it only has access to public members (and internal ones within the same module).

nezeri.q: Where can you declare extensions?
opts: At the top level (directly in a file), inside a class, or inside a function
nezeri.exp: The most common form is a top-level declaration — usually collected in a separate file like Genislenmeler.kt.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: An ikiqat() function has been added to the Int type. this is the receiver, i.e. 21. The result is 42.

nezeri.q: Why are extensions useful?
opts: They let you call helper functions with natural syntax
nezeri.exp: Instead of Komekci.qisalt(metn, 10), you can write metn.qisalt(10). The code becomes more readable and chainable.

nezeri.q: What do you need in order to use an extension?
opts: To import it if it's in another package
nezeri.exp: An extension belongs to a package, just like a regular top-level function. To use it from another package, you have to import it.

nezeri.q: How are extensions resolved?
opts: Statically — by the DECLARED type of the variable
nezeri.exp: The compiler turns an extension into a regular static function call. That's why polymorphism doesn't work here — this is the most commonly misunderstood point.

nezeri.q: If the class has a member method with the same signature, which one runs?
opts: The member method always takes precedence
nezeri.exp: The member method wins and the extension is never called. You don't get an error either — it's a source of silent bugs.

nezeri.q: Can you write an extension for a nullable type?
nezeri.code: fun String?.bosdurmu() = this == null || isEmpty()
opts: Yes — the receiver can be null, and checking it is the function's own job
nezeri.exp: When the receiver is declared nullable, you can call the function without a safe call. isNullOrEmpty() in the standard library is written exactly this way.

nezeri.q: How do you write a generic extension?
nezeri.exp: The type parameter is declared right after the fun keyword. This makes the function work for every element type.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: Static resolution: the variable is declared with the type Ana, so Ana.ad() is chosen. The actual type isn't taken into account.

nezeri.q: How do you declare an extension property?
nezeri.exp: Since there's no backing field, you can't assign a value directly — you must write a getter.

nezeri.q: How does an extension function look from Java?
opts: Like a static function — the receiver becomes the first parameter
nezeri.exp: fun String.f() becomes a static method FaylKt.f(String receiver) in Java. That's also why extensions are resolved statically.

nezeri.q: Can you use an extension function in a chain?
opts: Yes — if the result has a suitable type, it chains like a regular function
nezeri.exp: Chains like metn.qisalt(10).uppercase() are completely normal. This is the main appeal of extensions.

nezeri.q: Can you declare a local extension inside a function?
opts: Yes — it's visible only in that function
nezeri.exp: A local extension limits the scope and is handy for helper logic that's needed in only one place.

nezeri.q: Can you write an extension for a companion object?
nezeri.code:
class A { companion object }
fun A.Companion.yarat() = "yaradildi"
opts: Yes — it's called as A.yarat(), but the class must declare a companion
nezeri.exp: The class must have a companion object, even an empty one — otherwise there's no receiver for the extension. This lets you add factory methods from outside.

nezeri.q: Why is it recommended to collect extensions in a separate file?
opts: So they're easy to find and import
nezeri.exp: Files like Genislenmeler.kt or StringExt.kt give the project a single place for them. Otherwise the same extension gets duplicated in several places.

nezeri.q: How is a lambda with receiver (String.() -> Unit) related to extensions?
opts: It's the same principle — inside the lambda, this is the receiver; it's the foundation of DSLs
nezeri.exp: Functions like apply and buildString take exactly this kind of lambda with receiver. That's what makes HTML/Gradle-style DSLs possible.

nezeri.q: Can an extension override a member method?
opts: No — extensions can neither be overridden nor override anything
nezeri.exp: An extension isn't part of the class hierarchy. It neither overrides nor gets overridden — it's just a static function.

nezeri.q: Which function in the standard library is an extension?
nezeri.exp: Most collection operations and scope functions are written as extensions. That's why interfaces stay simple while the functionality stays rich.

nezeri.q: What happens if two different packages have an extension with the same name?
opts: Whichever one is imported is the one that runs
nezeri.exp: The import decides. If you need both, use an alias: import paket.f as digerF.

nezeri.q: When should you write a member method instead of an extension?
opts: A member method if the function needs access to the class's internal state
nezeri.exp: Behavior that works with private fields or has to be polymorphic should be a member method. An extension is for helper, external functionality.

nezeri.exp: The type parameter is written in angle brackets after the class name and can be used anywhere in the class.

nezeri.q: What does the letter T stand for?
opts: A type parameter — it can be any type
nezeri.exp: T is just a conventional name (Type). You can use any name: E (element), K/V (key/value), R (result).

nezeri.q: In the call Qutu("Kotlin"), what does T become?
opts: String — the compiler infers it from the argument
nezeri.exp: Type inference works with generics too. You can also write it explicitly: Qutu<String>("Kotlin").

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: T is inferred as Int, and the function returns the first element of the list.

nezeri.q: How do you put a constraint on a generic type?
nezeri.exp: The upper bound is written after a colon. After that, you can use that type's methods on T.

nezeri.q: If no constraint is written, what is T's upper bound?
nezeri.exp: The default upper bound is Any?, so T can also be nullable. To require a non-null type, write <T : Any>.

nezeri.q: How many type parameters are there in Map<K, V>?
nezeri.exp: K is the type of the key, and V is the type of the value. A class can have any number of type parameters.

nezeri.q: How do you write multiple constraints?
nezeri.exp: A single constraint can be written in the angle brackets; for more than one, you use a where clause after the function signature.

nezeri.q: What does out T mean?
opts: T is only used as a parameter
nezeri.exp: With a covariant type, a Qutu<It> value can be passed where a Qutu<Heyvan> is expected, because reading is safe. List<out E> is exactly like this.

nezeri.q: What does in T mean?
nezeri.exp: With a contravariant type, a Hedef<Heyvan> value can be passed where a Hedef<It> is expected. Comparable<in T> is an example of this.

nezeri.q: Why is MutableList<E> invariant?
opts: It's both read and written — if it were covariant, you could add the wrong type
nezeri.exp: If we accepted a MutableList<It> value as a MutableList<Heyvan>, it would be possible to add a Pisik to it. That's why mutable collections are invariant.

nezeri.q: What does the PECS rule mean?
nezeri.exp: If you only read from a type (producer), write out; if you only write to it (consumer), write in. If you need both, it stays invariant.

nezeri.q: When do you use a star projection (<*>)?
opts: When the type argument is unknown, but you know there is one
nezeri.exp: List<*> accepts a list with any element type. Elements are read as Any?, and adding is not possible.

nezeri.q: Are generic types kept at runtime on the JVM?
nezeri.exp: After compilation, List<String> becomes just List. That's why you can't write x is T in a regular function.

nezeri.q: What is reified needed for?
opts: To make the type available at runtime in an inline function
nezeri.exp: Because the body of an inline function is copied to the call site, the compiler can replace T with a concrete type. When that happens, x is T and T::class work.

nezeri.q: Which keyword is required together with reified?
nezeri.exp: reified is only possible in inline functions — the mechanism relies on the body being expanded at the call site.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?

nezeri.q: Can you assign listOf<It>() to a List<Heyvan> variable?
nezeri.exp: List is a read-only interface, so it's declared covariant. This makes everyday code much more convenient.

nezeri.q: How do you require a generic type to be non-nullable?
nezeri.exp: Any is the parent of all non-nullable types. If you write <T : Any>, a nullable type isn't accepted as T.

nezeri.q: How do you write a generic extension function?
nezeri.exp: The type parameter is declared after fun, before the receiver type.

nezeri.q: Can you use an out type as a function parameter?
opts: No — it causes a compilation error
nezeri.exp: out guarantees that the type only appears in output positions. Using it as a parameter would break that guarantee, so the compiler doesn't allow it. The only exception is private members.

nezeri.q: Can you create an object from a type parameter in a generic class (T())?
opts: No — type erasure doesn't allow it; you pass a factory lambda
nezeri.exp: Since T isn't known at runtime, the constructor can't be found. Usually a factory function of type () -> T is passed as a parameter.

nezeri.q: When does type inference happen for generic types?
opts: At compile time — from the arguments or the expected type
nezeri.exp: The compiler determines T by looking at both the arguments and the type of the variable the result is assigned to.

nezeri.q: Does Kotlin have checked exceptions?
opts: No — no method is forced to declare throws
nezeri.exp: Kotlin dropped one of Java's most criticized features. Catching or declaring an exception is entirely optional.

nezeri.q: How do you throw an exception?
nezeri.exp: You use the throw keyword. In Kotlin, throw is an expression, and its type is Nothing.

nezeri.q: Which part of a try block ALWAYS runs?
nezeri.exp: finally runs whether an exception is thrown or not. It's used to close resources — but in Kotlin, use() is better for that.

nezeri.q: What is try in Kotlin?
opts: An expression that returns a value
nezeri.exp: val n = try { "42".toInt() } catch (e: Exception) { 0 } — the last expression of the try block becomes the result.

nezeri.q: What does "abc".toInt() do?
nezeri.exp: When the conversion isn't possible, an exception is thrown. The safe option is toIntOrNull().

nezeri.q: How do you write the exception type in a catch block?
nezeri.exp: In Kotlin, the variable name comes first and the type after — just like function parameters.

nezeri.q: Which one is the common parent of all exceptions?
nezeri.exp: Exception and Error derive from Throwable. You usually catch Exception — Error signals system-level problems and shouldn't be caught.

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: The conversion fails, the catch block runs, and its last expression (-1) becomes the result.

nezeri.q: How many catch blocks can a single try block have?
opts: As many as you want — for different types
nezeri.exp: The branches are checked from top to bottom. More specific types should be written higher up, otherwise the general type will swallow them.

nezeri.q: Which exception does require() throw?
nezeri.exp: require() checks arguments — if the input is invalid, an IllegalArgumentException is thrown.

nezeri.q: Which exception does check() throw?
nezeri.exp: check() checks the object's internal state. If the state is invalid, an IllegalStateException is thrown.

nezeri.q: What does error("mesaj") do?
nezeri.exp: Its return type is Nothing, so it can be used on the right side of the Elvis operator: x ?: error("tapilmadi").

nezeri.q: What does TODO() do?
nezeri.exp: It's for marking code that hasn't been written yet. Since its type is Nothing, it can stand in for any return type.

nezeri.q: What does runCatching { } return?
nezeri.exp: It stores either the successful result or the caught exception in a Result object. You handle it with getOrNull(), getOrDefault(), onSuccess/onFailure.

nezeri.q: How do you create your own exception?
nezeri.exp: You inherit from Exception or one of its subclasses. The message is passed to the constructor: class Xeta(m: String) : Exception(m).

nezeri.q: What is the result of this code?
nezeri.exp: try starts (A), an exception is thrown, catch runs (B), and then finally always runs (C).

nezeri.q: Why is writing return inside finally dangerous?
opts: It swallows the thrown exception and hides the error
nezeri.exp: A return in finally cancels the exception, and the function returns normally. The problem silently disappears — this leads to bugs that are hard to find.

nezeri.q: What is the use() function for?
nezeri.exp: It's the counterpart of Java's try-with-resources: fayl.use { ... } — when the block ends, the resource is closed even if there's an exception.

nezeri.q: What is the @Throws annotation for?
opts: So that the Java side sees a checked exception
nezeri.exp: Kotlin has no checked exceptions. If you want Java code to require a try/catch, you mark the function with @Throws.

nezeri.q: When should you use an exception, and when a sealed result type?
opts: sealed/Result for expected failures, exceptions for programmer errors
nezeri.exp: No network, or failed validation — these are part of the business logic and should be expressed with types. A broken config or a null id, on the other hand, calls for an exception.

nezeri.q: Why is an empty catch block bad?
opts: It completely hides the error — the problem shows up later somewhere else
nezeri.exp: If the exception is swallowed, the program keeps running in an invalid state. At the very least, you should log it or rethrow it.

nezeri.q: How do you rethrow an exception?
nezeri.exp: After handling it in the catch block, writing throw e passes the exception up. In coroutines, CancellationException must always be passed on this way.

nezeri.q: What does Result.fold() do?
opts: Handles the success and failure cases in a single expression
nezeri.exp: fold(onSuccess = { ... }, onFailure = { ... }) — handles both cases in one place and returns a single value.

nezeri.q: What is the type of a throw expression?
nezeri.exp: Nothing is a type that has no values, and it's a subtype of all types. That's why the construct val x = y ?: throw Xeta() passes type checking.

nezeri.q: When does writing a general catch (e: Exception) cause problems?
opts: It also swallows unexpected errors and makes diagnosis harder
nezeri.exp: It's better to catch a specific type. If you do need a general catch, you should at least log it or rethrow it.

nezeri.q: What is property delegation?
opts: Handing the get/set logic over to another object
nezeri.exp: val x by delegate — read and write operations are passed to the delegate's getValue/setValue methods.

nezeri.q: What does by lazy do?
opts: Delays the value and never computes it
Computes it once on first access, then caches it
nezeri.exp: Ideal for heavy computations — if the value is never needed, it's never created.

nezeri.q: Which keyword can by lazy be used with?
nezeri.exp: lazy computes the value once and stores it, so it only makes sense with val. For var there's Delegates.observable or notNull.

nezeri.q: Is lazy thread-safe by default?
opts: Yes — SYNCHRONIZED mode is the default
nezeri.exp: The default mode applies synchronization. If it will only be used on a single thread, LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE is faster.

nezeri.q: What does Delegates.observable do?
nezeri.exp: The lambda receives the old and new value. The change has already happened — it can't be undone.

nezeri.q: What does Delegates.vetoable do?
nezeri.exp: The lambda returns a Boolean: if it returns false, the new value isn't assigned and the property keeps its old value.

nezeri.q: What is Delegates.notNull() for?
opts: A replacement for lateinit with primitive types
nezeri.exp: lateinit doesn't work with primitive types like Int and Double. notNull() fills that gap.

nezeri.q: How is the result of a by lazy block determined?
opts: The last expression of the block
nezeri.exp: It works like a lambda — the last expression becomes the property's value.

nezeri.q: How many times is "hesablanir" printed by this code?
nezeri.exp: lazy computes the value only on first access. On the second access the cached value is returned.

nezeri.q: Why is delegating to a Map useful?
opts: To build an object directly from a JSON or config map
nezeri.exp: class A(m: Map<String, Any?>) { val ad: String by m } — the property name is used as the key and the value is read from the map.

nezeri.q: Which operator functions do you need to write your own delegate?
nezeri.exp: For val you declare only getValue(); for var you declare both getValue() and setValue() — both must be operator.

nezeri.q: What are the parameters of getValue()?
nezeri.exp: The first parameter is the object that owns the property, and the second is metadata about the property (its name, type).

nezeri.q: How many parameters does setValue() take?
nezeri.exp: The owner, the property metadata and the new value — three parameters.

nezeri.q: What does by do at the class level?
opts: Hands the interface implementation over to another object
nezeri.exp: class A(d: Cap) : Cap by d — all interface methods are automatically forwarded to the d object. It makes composition easier.

nezeri.q: What does lazy's PUBLICATION mode mean?
opts: Several threads may compute it, the first result is kept
Each thread gets its own copy
nezeri.exp: The computation may run more than once, but the result is a single one. It's used to avoid synchronization overhead when the computation is cheap.

nezeri.q: How many parameters does the observable lambda take?
nezeri.exp: Usually the first parameter isn't needed and is discarded with an underscore: { _, kohne, yeni -> ... }

nezeri.q: How do you declare an annotation?
nezeri.exp: You use the annotation class keyword. Its parameters are defined in the constructor and can only be constant values.

nezeri.q: What does the @Target annotation do?
opts: Restricts which elements the annotation can be placed on
nezeri.exp: @Target(AnnotationTarget.CLASS, AnnotationTarget.FUNCTION) — the annotation can only be placed on classes and functions.

nezeri.q: What does @Retention define?
opts: How long it's kept — in the source, in the bytecode, or at runtime
nezeri.exp: Without RUNTIME you can't read it via reflection. The default value is RUNTIME.

nezeri.q: What does the @Deprecated annotation do?
opts: Marks it as deprecated and can suggest a replacement
nezeri.exp: With the ReplaceWith parameter the IDE offers an automatic fix. The level parameter can turn the warning into an error.

nezeri.q: Why is reflection expensive in Kotlin?
opts: The kotlin-reflect dependency is large and it's slow at runtime
nezeri.exp: On Android it's recommended to avoid it. Compiler plugins like kotlinx.serialization do the same job without reflection.

nezeri.q: Can a delegate class be generic?
opts: Yes — it can be reused for any type
nezeri.exp: class Loglayan<T>(private var d: T) — one delegate works for every type. The delegates in the standard library are like that too.

nezeri.q: What is the ReadWriteProperty interface for?
opts: A ready-made delegate contract for var properties
nezeri.exp: If you implement it, the compiler checks the getValue and setValue signatures. For val there's the matching ReadOnlyProperty.

nezeri.q: What's the main difference between lateinit and by lazy?
opts: lateinit is for var and is set from outside; lazy is for val and computes the value itself
nezeri.exp: lateinit doesn't know who will provide the value, and it isn't checked. lazy computes the value itself and it's always available.

nezeri.q: What is a coroutine?
opts: A lightweight task that can be suspended and resumed
nezeri.exp: A coroutine doesn't hold an operating system resource. Hundreds of thousands of coroutines can run on just a few threads.

nezeri.q: What does the suspend keyword mean?
opts: The function can be suspended — it's only called inside a coroutine
The function creates a new thread
nezeri.exp: A suspend function can pause without blocking the thread. You can only call it from another suspend function or from a coroutine builder.

nezeri.q: What's the difference between delay() and Thread.sleep()?
opts: delay doesn't block the thread, sleep does
nezeri.exp: That's the whole difference: delay only suspends the coroutine, while the thread is freed up to run other coroutines.

nezeri.q: What does runBlocking do?
opts: Creates a coroutine and blocks the current thread
nezeri.exp: It's a bridge from regular code into the coroutine world. It's used in main() and in tests, but you should avoid it in production code.

nezeri.q: What does launch return?
nezeri.exp: launch is for "fire and forget" — it doesn't return a result. With the Job you can wait for the coroutine (join) or cancel it (cancel).

nezeri.q: What does async return?
opts: Deferred<T> — the result is obtained with await()
nezeri.exp: Deferred is the result-returning variant of Job. await() waits until the result is ready without blocking the thread.

nezeri.q: Can you call a suspend function from a regular function?
opts: No — you need a coroutine scope
nezeri.exp: The compiler reports an error. As a bridge you use runBlocking, or launch/async of an existing scope.

nezeri.q: What does this code print?
nezeri.exp: The code runs sequentially: A is printed, it waits 100 ms, then B. delay doesn't block the thread, it just suspends the coroutine.

nezeri.q: What does job.join() do?
nezeri.exp: The waiting doesn't block the thread. If you need a result, use async and await().

nezeri.q: Does awaiting two asyncs one after the other give you parallelism?
opts: Yes — both start as soon as async is called
nezeri.exp: async starts the work immediately, and await just waits for the result. So the total time is as long as the longest task.

nezeri.q: What does coroutineScope do?
opts: Waits until all child coroutines finish
nezeri.exp: It's the foundation of structured concurrency: no child is left "lost" before the scope finishes.

nezeri.q: What is Dispatchers.IO for?
opts: Network, files, databases — work with a lot of waiting
nezeri.exp: The IO pool has 64+ threads, because this kind of work mostly waits. For CPU-intensive work you use Dispatchers.Default.

nezeri.q: What does withContext do?
opts: Runs the block on another dispatcher and returns the result
nezeri.exp: It's the standard way to switch dispatchers: withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { faylOxu() }.

nezeri.q: What does structured concurrency mean?
opts: Every coroutine belongs to a scope, and when the scope is cancelled they all stop
nezeri.exp: This prevents "lost" tasks. When a ViewModel is destroyed, all the work in viewModelScope stops automatically.

nezeri.q: What is a Flow?
opts: An asynchronous stream that emits several values over time
nezeri.exp: A suspend function returns one value, while a Flow emits many values in sequence. You read it with collect.

nezeri.q: When does the computation in a Flow start?
nezeri.exp: A Flow is cold — nothing runs until collect, the terminal operation, is called.

nezeri.q: How does coroutine cancellation work?
opts: It requires cooperation — it only happens at a suspension point
An exception is thrown and swallowed
nezeri.exp: It's checked at suspension points like delay, yield and withContext. If a long CPU loop has no suspension point, cancellation doesn't work — you need to add ensureActive().

nezeri.q: What should you do with a CancellationException caught in a catch block?
nezeri.exp: The cancellation mechanism relies on this exception being propagated upward. If it's swallowed, the coroutine isn't considered cancelled and the scope keeps waiting.

nezeri.q: How does supervisorScope differ from coroutineScope?
opts: An error in one child doesn't stop the other children
nezeri.exp: In coroutineScope, when one child crashes, all its siblings are cancelled. In supervisorScope, each child is independent.

nezeri.q: What's the difference between StateFlow and Flow?
opts: StateFlow is hot and always holds the current value
nezeri.exp: StateFlow is for UI state — a subscriber immediately gets the latest value. For one-off events you use SharedFlow.

nezeri.q: Why shouldn't runBlocking be used in production code?
opts: It blocks the current thread — cancelling out all the benefits of coroutines
nezeri.exp: Its name says it all. It's only appropriate in main(), in tests, and as a bridge to legacy code.

nezeri.q: What does awaitAll() do?
nezeri.exp: listOf(a, b, c).awaitAll() — more readable than writing sequential awaits, and if any of them crashes it fails immediately.

nezeri.q: What is yield() for?
opts: Giving other coroutines a turn and creating a cancellation point
nezeri.exp: Calling yield() or ensureActive() in a long computation loop makes cancellation possible.

nezeri.q: What is Kotlin's standard test library?
nezeri.exp: kotlin.test provides platform-independent assert functions. On the JVM, JUnit runs underneath, but your code stays the same.

nezeri.q: What is the order of assertEquals() parameters?
nezeri.exp: You write the expected value first, then the actual one. The wrong order flips the error message and makes diagnosis harder.

nezeri.q: How is a test function marked?
nezeri.exp: The @Test annotation comes from the kotlin.test package and makes the function visible to the test runner.

nezeri.q: What do you do to use spaces in a test name?
nezeri.exp: fun `bos siyahi ucun null qaytarir`() — tests read like sentences and serve as documentation.

nezeri.q: What does assertTrue() check?
nezeri.exp: If the condition is false, an AssertionError is thrown. Its opposite is assertFalse().

nezeri.q: What happens when an assert fails?
nezeri.exp: AssertionError derives from Throwable. The test runner catches it and marks the test as failed.

nezeri.q: What does @BeforeTest do?
nezeri.exp: It's for setting up a clean initial state for every test. Its counterpart is @AfterTest.

nezeri.q: What does assertNull() check?
nezeri.exp: Its pair is assertNotNull(), which both checks and returns the value with a non-null type.

nezeri.q: What does this code do?
nezeri.exp: The expected and actual values are the same, so the assert passes silently and the next line runs.

nezeri.q: What is assertFailsWith for?
opts: Checking that a specific exception is thrown
nezeri.exp: assertFailsWith<NumberFormatException> { ... } — it both checks that the exception was thrown and returns the exception object so you can check the message too.

nezeri.q: When is assertContentEquals used?
opts: To compare the contents of collections and arrays
nezeri.exp: For arrays, assertEquals compares references and gives the wrong result. To compare contents you need assertContentEquals.

nezeri.q: What does the AAA pattern stand for?
nezeri.exp: Setup, execution, verification. Splitting a test into three clear parts makes it readable and easier to diagnose.

nezeri.q: How many behaviors should one test check?
opts: One — that way the cause of a failure is immediately clear
nezeri.exp: When a test that checks many things fails, it's hard to find which part broke. The one test, one assertion principle works.

nezeri.q: What do you use for coroutine tests?
opts: runTest — it skips delays instantly with virtual time
nezeri.exp: runTest is in the kotlinx-coroutines-test package. delay(5000) doesn't take a real 5 seconds — virtual time is moved forward.

nezeri.q: What is a mock?
opts: A fake object that replaces a real dependency in a test
nezeri.exp: It replaces heavy dependencies like the network or a database. In Kotlin MockK is used most often, because it also works with final classes.

nezeri.q: What do you use in MockK to mock a suspend function?
nezeri.exp: coEvery and coVerify are for suspend functions. For regular functions you use every and verify.

nezeri.q: What's the difference between assertSame() and assertEquals()?
opts: assertSame checks the reference, assertEquals checks the content
nezeri.exp: assertSame works like the triple equals sign. Usually you need a content comparison, so assertEquals is used more often.

nezeri.q: Why are backtick names used in test code?
opts: To express what the test checks as a sentence
nezeri.exp: The name shows up as-is in the test report. A good name explains what the test does without reading it.

nezeri.q: What is a parameterized test for?
opts: Checking the same logic with different sets of inputs
nezeri.exp: With @ParameterizedTest and @CsvSource, one test function covers dozens of cases. Duplicate code goes away.

nezeri.q: What is the most important principle for writing testable code?
opts: Passing dependencies in from outside (dependency injection)
nezeri.exp: If a class creates its own dependency internally, you can't replace it in a test. Passing it through the constructor makes testing easier.

nezeri.q: What is the Turbine library for?
nezeri.exp: It lets you check the values a Flow emits one by one: awaitItem(), awaitComplete().

nezeri.q: What does 100% test coverage guarantee?
opts: Only that every line ran at least once — not correctness
nezeri.exp: A line can run without its result being checked. Coverage is a useful metric, not a goal.

nezeri.q: Why is it bad to make real network requests in a test?
opts: It's slow and unstable — the result depends on external factors
nezeri.exp: Such a test sometimes passes and sometimes doesn't — it becomes flaky. In unit tests the network is mocked, and real integration is checked in a separate test suite.

nezeri.q: What does assertFailsWith return?
nezeri.exp: On the returned object you can check the message or its own fields — this makes the test more precise.

nezeri.q: What should a test name reflect?
opts: The condition, the action and the expected result
nezeri.exp: A name like "bos siyahi ucun null qaytarir" (returns null for an empty list) fully explains what the test checks. "test1" says nothing.

nezeri.q: Can Kotlin and Java work together in the same project?
opts: Yes — they compile to the same bytecode
nezeri.exp: There's full interoperability. A Kotlin file can use a Java class directly, and a Java file can use a Kotlin class directly.

nezeri.q: Are semicolons mandatory in Kotlin?
nezeri.exp: In Java they're mandatory after every statement, while in Kotlin you almost never need them.

nezeri.q: What is the Kotlin equivalent of a Java POJO class?
nezeri.exp: In Java it's 50+ lines (fields, getters/setters, equals, hashCode, toString) — in Kotlin it's one line.

nezeri.q: What is the Kotlin equivalent of Java's static members?
opts: companion object or a top-level declaration
nezeri.exp: Kotlin has no static keyword. Members tied to a class go in a companion object, while standalone functions are written directly in the file.

nezeri.q: How does Kotlin's == operator differ from Java's?
opts: In Kotlin it compares content, in Java it compares references
nezeri.exp: In Java you have to write equals() when comparing strings. In Kotlin == already calls equals() — this eliminates a classic bug.

nezeri.q: What is the Kotlin equivalent of a Java final variable?
nezeri.exp: val is read-only. In Java writing final is optional, while in Kotlin using val is the standard approach.

nezeri.q: What are classes like in Kotlin by default?
nezeri.exp: In Java classes are open for inheritance by default. Kotlin chose the opposite: inheritance has to be allowed deliberately.

nezeri.q: What is the Kotlin equivalent of Java's switch?
nezeri.exp: when accepts any type, ranges and type checks, and returns a value. You don't need to write break either.

nezeri.q: Does Kotlin have the ternary operator (a ? b : c)?
opts: No — the if expression replaces it
nezeri.exp: Since if itself returns a value, there's no need for a separate operator: val m = if (a > b) a else b.

nezeri.q: Which language has checked exceptions?
nezeri.exp: Kotlin dropped checked exceptions. When you call a Java method, you're not forced to write try/catch.

nezeri.q: How do types coming from Java look in Kotlin?
opts: A platform type (String!) — the compiler doesn't check it
nezeri.exp: Java has no null information. That's why it's safe to treat values coming from Java APIs as nullable.

nezeri.q: What does @JvmStatic do?
opts: Makes a companion member truly static for Java
nezeri.exp: Without it, on the Java side you have to write Sinif.Companion.metod(). With the annotation, Sinif.metod() becomes possible.

nezeri.q: What is @JvmOverloads for?
opts: Generating Java overloads for default parameters
nezeri.exp: Java doesn't know about default parameters. This annotation generates a separate method for each parameter combination.

nezeri.q: What is the Kotlin equivalent of a Java util class?
nezeri.exp: Instead of StringUtils.qisalt(s, 10), you can write an extension and say s.qisalt(10). There's no need to wrap it in a class.

nezeri.q: Does Kotlin have primitive types?
opts: Yes, int and Integer are separate
No — there's only Int, and the compiler converts it to a primitive when needed
Everything is an object and isn't optimized
nezeri.exp: Java has the int/Integer split. Kotlin hides it: when an Int isn't nullable, it's stored as a primitive int on the JVM.

nezeri.q: What's the difference between Java's String.format() and a Kotlin template?
opts: A template puts the variable straight into the text and is more readable
nezeri.exp: In the form "Salam, $ad!" the variable is written directly. You don't have to keep track of parameter order as you do with format strings.

nezeri.q: How close is a Java 21 record to Kotlin's data class?
opts: Close — but there's no copy() and no named arguments
nezeri.exp: A Java record generates equals/hashCode/toString, but it lacks Kotlin's copy() method and default/named arguments.

nezeri.q: How does a top-level function in a Kotlin file look from Java?
opts: As a static method of the FaylAdiKt class
nezeri.exp: Functions in the Komekci.kt file are gathered in the KomekciKt class. You can change the name with @file:JvmName.

nezeri.q: What's the best strategy for moving from Java to Kotlin?
opts: Starting with tests and new files, and expanding gradually
Using it only in new projects
nezeri.exp: The two languages live side by side in the same project without problems. A big rewrite is risky and unnecessary — model classes are the starting point with the biggest payoff.

nezeri.q: What do you need to do after the IDE's automatic Java→Kotlin conversion?
opts: Clean up by hand — the converter leaves lots of !! and unnecessary type declarations
nezeri.exp: The converter plays it safe and puts !! everywhere. You need to replace them with ?. and ?:, otherwise you lose the benefit of null safety.

nezeri.q: What does @JvmField do?
opts: Exposes the property directly as a field, without a getter/setter
nezeri.exp: From the Java side, direct access in the form obyekt.xasse becomes possible. It's used in performance-critical places or for API compatibility.

nezeri.q: How does Kotlin's performance compare to Java's?
opts: Practically the same — it compiles to the same bytecode
nezeri.exp: The difference isn't measurable. Compilation time used to be a problem; the K2 compiler solved that.

nezeri.q: How do you write the equivalent of a Java static initializer block in Kotlin?
nezeri.exp: A companion object is itself an object, so it can have an init block too, which runs once on first access.

nezeri.q: What is the Kotlin equivalent of Java's Optional?
opts: A nullable type (T?) — built into the language
nezeri.exp: Because Kotlin bakes null safety into the type system, there's no need for a separate wrapper class. This is both more concise and faster.

nezeri.q: Will Kotlin replace Java?
opts: On Android it practically has, while on the backend Java will stay for a long time
nezeri.exp: Since 2019 Google has followed a "Kotlin-first" policy for Android. On the backend, Java's ecosystem and stability remain strong — the two aren't rivals.

opts: var — you can make it val later
val — switch to var only when needed
nezeri.exp: Immutability should be the default. When you start with val, the compiler prevents accidental changes and the code is easier to follow.

nezeri.q: What is the most idiomatic form of a null check?
nezeri.exp: Combining a safe call with let is both short and gives you a non-null type inside the block. In simple cases, if is perfectly fine too.

nezeri.q: What is used to provide a fallback value?
nezeri.exp: The Elvis operator is the standard form of this pattern and reads in a single line.

nezeri.q: What is recommended for processing a collection?
nezeri.exp: A chain says what it does, while a loop says how it does it. The former is more readable and less error-prone.

nezeri.q: What is the most idiomatic way to build an object?
nezeri.exp: Inside apply you use this, and at the end the object itself is returned — ideal for the builder style.

nezeri.q: When should a single-expression function be used?
opts: When the body consists of a single expression
nezeri.exp: fun kvadrat(x: Int) = x * x — no need to write curly braces and return.

nezeri.q: What should function names be like?
opts: A verb — it should say what the function does
nezeri.exp: hesabla(), yukle(), tesdiqle() — it's clear what they do. data() or info() say nothing.

nezeri.q: What should a Boolean variable name be like?
nezeri.exp: The name itself should answer a true/false question. if (aktivdir) is readable, while if (status) is ambiguous.

nezeri.q: What is the problem with this code?
nezeri.code: val netice = if (x > 5) true else false
opts: It's unnecessary — x > 5 already returns a Boolean
nezeri.exp: This is a classic code smell. Simply writing val netice = x > 5 is enough.

nezeri.q: How should you fix deeply nested if blocks?
opts: Early return or a when without an argument
nezeri.exp: An early return in the form val x = giris ?: return flattens the code. Deeply nested blocks create a «pyramid».

nezeri.q: What is recommended for a multi-step chain on a large collection?
opts: asSequence() — no intermediate lists are created
nezeri.exp: Each step doesn't create a new list; elements flow through one by one. For small collections, though, a regular List is faster.

nezeri.q: What should be used instead of concatenating strings inside a loop?
nezeri.exp: Since String is immutable, every concatenation creates a new object. buildString works with a single StringBuilder.

nezeri.q: What is recommended when a function has more than three parameters?
opts: Use named arguments in the call
nezeri.exp: yarat(true, false, true) tells you nothing six months later. yarat(gorunen = true, aktiv = false), on the other hand, explains itself.

nezeri.q: How should data classes be kept?
opts: As immutable as possible — all properties val
nezeri.exp: Immutable objects are thread-safe and protect against unexpected changes. If you need a change, use copy().

nezeri.q: Where should extension functions be kept?
opts: Gathered in one place — for example Genislenmeler.kt
nezeri.exp: Without a single place, the same extension gets duplicated in several places and becomes hard to find.

nezeri.q: How many levels of nested scope functions are acceptable?
opts: Two at most — after that readability is lost
nezeri.exp: In nested blocks, this and it get mixed up. When it gets deeper, a plain variable and an if are clearer.

nezeri.q: What should be used instead of strings for a fixed set of values?
nezeri.exp: A typo in a string constant passes compilation. With an enum, the compiler checks every case.

nezeri.q: What is used for a collection operation whose result you don't need?
nezeri.exp: map creates a new list — if you don't need the result, that wastes memory. forEach exists for side effects.

nezeri.q: When is the not-null assertion operator (!!) acceptable?
opts: Almost never — each one is a potential crash
nezeri.exp: When you see !! in code, ask: why can't this value be null? If there's an answer, make the type non-null from the start.

nezeri.q: Why is returning a MutableList from an API bad?
opts: The caller can change the internal state
nezeri.exp: Returning a copy with toList() preserves encapsulation. Just declaring the type as List isn't enough — the underlying object is still mutable.

nezeri.q: What do ktlint and detekt do?
opts: They automatically check formatting and code smells
nezeri.exp: Once they're hooked into CI, style discussions disappear from code reviews entirely — the focus shifts to logic.

nezeri.q: What is recommended for id types?

nezeri.q: Which approach is recommended for heavy objects?
opts: by lazy — if it isn't needed, it's never created
nezeri.exp: Lazy initialization both shortens startup time and avoids creating resources that are never used.

nezeri.q: When should the return type be written explicitly in a public API?
opts: Always — it improves readability and prevents accidental changes
nezeri.exp: Type inference is great for local variables. But in a public function, when you change the body, the return type can silently change too — and that breaks the API.

nezeri.q: What is the most important rule for code readability?

It should have lots of comments
It should be on one line
nezeri.exp: An overly compressed chain may be short, but it becomes unreadable. Giving an intermediate variable a name is often better.

nezeri.q: Which language does Google recommend for Android?
nezeri.exp: New Android APIs are designed for Kotlin first. Most of the Jetpack libraries are written in Kotlin.

nezeri.q: What is Jetpack Compose?
nezeri.exp: Instead of XML layouts, the UI is described directly with Kotlin functions. When the state changes, the interface updates automatically.

nezeri.q: What does a @Composable function do?
opts: It describes a piece of UI
nezeri.exp: Composable functions don't return a result — they declare what should be added to the UI tree.

nezeri.q: What is a ViewModel for?
opts: Holding UI state so it isn't lost when the screen rotates
nezeri.exp: On a configuration change (screen rotation), the Activity is recreated, but the ViewModel survives.

nezeri.q: What does remember { mutableStateOf(0) } do?
opts: It creates state — when it changes, the UI is redrawn
nezeri.exp: mutableStateOf creates observable state, and remember keeps it across redraws.

nezeri.q: On which thread should the UI be updated in Android?
nezeri.exp: Touching the UI from another thread causes a crash. In coroutines, Dispatchers.Main is used.

nezeri.q: What is Room?
opts: A database library built on top of SQLite
nezeri.exp: It checks SQL queries at compile time and converts the results into Kotlin objects.

nezeri.q: What is Retrofit for?
nezeri.exp: You declare an interface, and Retrofit generates the implementation itself. It supports suspend functions directly.

nezeri.q: What is the most widely used architecture pattern in Android?
nezeri.exp: The View observes the state, the ViewModel holds the logic, and the Repository combines the data sources.

nezeri.q: When is viewModelScope cancelled?
opts: When the ViewModel is destroyed — all coroutines stop automatically
nezeri.exp: This is the practical benefit of structured concurrency: no leaks and no «lost» requests.

nezeri.q: What is recommended for modeling UI state?
opts: A sealed interface — Yuklenir, Ugurlu, Xeta
nezeri.exp: With separate flags, impossible combinations appear (both loading and error). sealed makes this impossible.

nezeri.q: Why is StateFlow a good fit for UI?
opts: It always holds the current value — a subscriber gets the latest state immediately
nezeri.exp: When a screen is recreated and subscribes, the latest state arrives immediately. For one-time events, SharedFlow is used instead.

nezeri.q: On which dispatcher should a network request run?
nezeri.exp: The IO pool is for work with a lot of waiting. To deliver the result to the UI, you switch back to Main.

nezeri.q: What do you get when a Room DAO returns a Flow?
opts: The UI updates automatically when the database changes
nezeri.exp: As soon as the table changes, the Flow emits a new list — there's no need to trigger a refresh manually.

nezeri.q: What is the Repository pattern for?
opts: Combining data sources (network, database) behind a single interface
nezeri.exp: The ViewModel doesn't know where the data comes from. This makes testing easier and makes it possible to swap the source.

nezeri.q: What happens in Compose when state changes?
opts: The composables that read that state are redrawn (recomposition)
nezeri.exp: Compose redraws only the affected parts — not the whole tree.

nezeri.q: What is used for dependency injection in Android?
nezeri.exp: It automates passing dependencies by hand and makes swapping them in tests easier.

nezeri.q: Why are extension functions used so much in Android?
opts: They let you add helper functions to framework classes (View, Context) without touching them
nezeri.exp: fun View.gorunsun() { visibility = View.VISIBLE } — you adapt the API to your needs without changing the framework class.

nezeri.q: Which scope should you use when running a long coroutine in an Activity?
nezeri.exp: GlobalScope is never cancelled and causes memory leaks. Lifecycle-bound scopes are cleaned up automatically.

nezeri.q: What is collectAsStateWithLifecycle() for?
opts: Stopping the flow while the screen is in the background
nezeri.exp: Plain collectAsState keeps running even when the screen isn't visible and wastes resources. The lifecycle variant solves this.

nezeri.q: How should UI state be exposed from a ViewModel?
opts: As a StateFlow — made read-only with asStateFlow()
nezeri.exp: A MutableStateFlow is kept inside, and a StateFlow that can't be changed is exposed outside — only the ViewModel changes the state.

nezeri.q: Why is state lifted up in Compose (state hoisting)?
opts: To make the Composable stateless and reusable
nezeri.exp: State is kept higher up and passed down as parameters. Such a component is testable and flexible.

nezeri.q: What should be used for a one-time event (toast, navigation)?
nezeri.exp: StateFlow keeps the last value — when the screen is recreated, the toast would be shown again. SharedFlow solves this problem.

nezeri.q: Why should you avoid reflection in Android?
opts: It's slow and increases the APK size
nezeri.exp: kotlin-reflect is about 3 MB. Compiler plugins like kotlinx.serialization do the same job without reflection.

nezeri.q: What is used for UI testing in the modern Android stack?
nezeri.exp: JUnit + MockK for unit tests, the Compose testing API or Espresso for UI, and Turbine for Flow.

nezeri.q: What is the main idea behind Kotlin Multiplatform?
opts: Making the UI the same everywhere
Writing the business logic once and keeping the interface native
nezeri.exp: KMP doesn't replace the UI. Logic such as networking, database and validation is shared, while the screens stay native on each platform.

nezeri.q: What is the commonMain folder for?
nezeri.exp: This is where platform-independent code is written. Platform-specific parts go into folders such as androidMain and iosMain.

nezeri.q: What does the expect keyword do?
opts: It declares only a signature in shared code
nezeri.exp: expect fun platformaAdi(): String — the shared code expects this function to exist, and each platform provides its own actual version.

nezeri.q: What does the actual keyword do?
nezeri.exp: Every target platform must provide an actual implementation matching the expect declaration — otherwise compilation fails.

nezeri.q: Which platforms does KMP support?
nezeri.exp: Behind the scenes, Kotlin/JVM, Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS compile for the different targets.

nezeri.q: What does Compose Multiplatform do?
opts: It lets you share the UI too
nezeri.exp: In plain KMP the UI stays native. Compose Multiplatform, on the other hand, shares the interface itself across Android, iOS, desktop and web.

nezeri.q: Which library is usually used for networking in KMP?
nezeri.exp: Retrofit is JVM-only. Ktor Client, however, is multiplatform and uses its own engine for each target.

nezeri.q: What is used for the database in KMP?
nezeri.exp: Room is tied to JVM/Android. SQLDelight generates multiplatform Kotlin code from SQL.

nezeri.q: How is KMP different from React Native?
opts: It doesn't replace the UI — the interface stays native
nezeri.exp: React Native builds the UI with its own components. KMP shares only the logic, and the screens are written natively in SwiftUI and Compose.

nezeri.q: What other approach can be used instead of expect/actual?
opts: An interface + a platform-specific implementation (dependency injection)
nezeri.exp: An interface is declared in shared code, and each platform provides its own class. This is more flexible than expect/actual and easier to test.

nezeri.q: Which code is suitable for sharing?
opts: Business logic, data models, validation, the network layer
nezeri.exp: Anything platform-independent can be shared. Deep OS integration, however, should stay native.

nezeri.q: Which code should be kept native?
opts: Permissions, camera, push notifications, payment integrations
nezeri.exp: These areas are tightly bound to platform APIs, and trying to share them brings more complexity than benefit.

nezeri.q: What is the commonTest folder for?
opts: Tests for shared code — they run on all platforms
nezeri.exp: A test written once runs on every target. That's why the kotlin.test library is platform-independent.

nezeri.q: What must the actual version of an expect class do?
opts: Only the name has to match
It must provide all expect members with the same signatures
It can have a different signature
nezeri.exp: If the signatures don't match, the compiler reports an error. This guarantees that the shared code will work on every platform.

nezeri.q: How are targets declared in Gradle in a KMP project?
opts: In the kotlin { androidTarget(); iosArm64(); jvm() } block
nezeri.exp: Each target gets its own source set and dependencies: commonMain, androidMain, iosMain.

nezeri.q: What is used for date/time in shared code?
nezeri.exp: java.time is JVM-only. kotlinx-datetime is multiplatform and can be used in shared code.

nezeri.q: What is used for JSON in KMP?
nezeri.exp: The others rely on reflection and only work on the JVM. Since kotlinx.serialization works through a compiler plugin, it's available on every platform.

nezeri.q: How is Kotlin code used on the iOS side?
opts: It's compiled as a framework and called from Swift
nezeri.exp: Kotlin/Native produces an Objective-C compatible framework for iOS. Swift code uses it like a regular library.

nezeri.q: Roughly how much code can be shared in KMP?
opts: 50-70% when sharing logic, 85-95% with Compose Multiplatform
nezeri.exp: The number depends on the project. In a UI-heavy app the share is smaller, in a logic-heavy app it's larger.

nezeri.q: What is the downside of expect/actual compared to the interface approach?
opts: It's hard to test — you can't swap the implementation
nezeri.exp: With the interface approach, it's easy to provide a fake implementation in tests. expect/actual, however, is bound at compile time.

nezeri.q: Can you use a platform-specific library in shared code?
nezeri.exp: commonMain only sees APIs that exist on all targets. Platform-specific code should go into the corresponding source set.

nezeri.q: What is the best starting point for adopting KMP?
opts: A small, clean part such as data models and validation logic
nezeri.exp: KMP can be added to an existing project gradually. Starting with a small, platform-independent module is risk-free.

nezeri.q: How does memory management work in Kotlin/Native?
opts: The new memory model has a GC and resembles the JVM
nezeri.exp: The old model had serious restrictions. The new memory model (the default since 1.7.20) removed them.

nezeri.q: Is it possible to write a shared ViewModel?
opts: Yes — the state and logic are shared, while the UI is native
nezeri.exp: The StateFlow lives in shared code, and Compose and SwiftUI subscribe to it. This is one of the places where KMP is most useful.

nezeri.q: Which part of KMP takes the most time?
opts: Build configuration and integrating the iOS side
nezeri.exp: The Kotlin code is usually trouble-free. Gradle targets, framework setup and Xcode integration need more attention.

nezeri.q: Who developed Ktor?
nezeri.exp: Ktor was written by JetBrains, the creator of Kotlin, and is fully Kotlin-based — coroutine support is native.

nezeri.q: How is a route declared in Ktor?
nezeri.exp: Ktor is DSL-based: inside the routing block you use the get, post, put and delete functions.

nezeri.q: How is a REST controller marked in Spring Boot?
nezeri.exp: @RestController writes each method's result directly into the response body — no separate @ResponseBody is needed.

nezeri.q: What does the HTTP 404 code mean?
nezeri.exp: 2xx is success, 4xx is a client error, 5xx is a server error. 404 means the requested resource doesn't exist.

nezeri.q: What does the HTTP 500 code mean?
nezeri.exp: The 5xx group indicates a problem in the server itself — the client can't fix it by correcting the request.

nezeri.q: What do you install for JSON support in Ktor?
nezeri.exp: install(ContentNegotiation) { json() } — after that, data classes are converted to JSON automatically.

nezeri.q: Which annotation is needed to convert a data class to JSON?
nezeri.exp: The kotlinx.serialization compiler plugin generates the serialization code itself based on the @Serializable marker — it doesn't use reflection.

nezeri.q: What is Ktor's advantage over Spring Boot?
opts: It's lightweight and starts very fast
nezeri.exp: Ktor starts in about 300 ms, while Spring takes 2-5 seconds. In microservices and serverless environments, this matters.

nezeri.q: What is Spring Boot's advantage over Ktor?
opts: A huge, mature ecosystem — lots of ready-made solutions
nezeri.exp: There are ready-made modules for security, batch processing and integrations. In an enterprise environment, that's a big advantage.

nezeri.q: How is a path parameter read in Ktor?
nezeri.exp: In the get("/istifadeciler/{id}") route, you use call.parameters["id"], and the result is a String?.

nezeri.q: How is a path parameter read in Spring?
nezeri.exp: @PathVariable reads a part of the path, while @RequestParam reads a parameter from the query string.

nezeri.q: What is Exposed?
nezeri.exp: It lets you write SQL queries with a Kotlin DSL — column names and types are checked at compile time.

nezeri.q: Can a suspend function be used inside a route in Ktor?
opts: Yes — route handlers are already in a suspend context
nezeri.exp: Ktor is entirely coroutine-based. A suspend call to the database or another service can be written directly.

nezeri.q: What is the POST method for in REST?
nezeri.exp: GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE deletes. A successful creation is usually answered with a 201 code.

nezeri.q: Which status code should be returned for invalid input?
nezeri.exp: 400 Bad Request means the request itself is wrong. 404, on the other hand, means the resource wasn't found.

nezeri.q: Where should validation happen in a backend?
opts: Always on the server — client validation is only for user convenience
nezeri.exp: Client code can be modified in any way. The server shouldn't trust any incoming data.

nezeri.q: What is used for error handling in Ktor?
nezeri.exp: StatusPages converts exceptions into status codes in a centralized way — no need to write try/catch again in every route.

nezeri.q: Why is splitting a project into layers important?
opts: When the route, service and repository are separate, testing and changes get easier
nezeri.exp: The route should deal only with HTTP, the business logic should live in the service, and data access in the repository.

nezeri.q: What is used for authentication in Ktor?
opts: The Authentication plugin — JWT, Basic, OAuth
nezeri.exp: install(Authentication) { jwt { ... } } — then routes are protected with an authenticate block.

nezeri.q: How should a blocking JDBC call be made inside a coroutine?
nezeri.exp: JDBC is blocking. Calling it directly blocks the coroutine's thread and reduces the throughput of the whole server.

nezeri.q: Why is it important to separate the DTO from the domain model in an API?
opts: So the API contract doesn't break when the internal model changes
nezeri.exp: The domain model changes according to internal needs. The DTO, however, is an external contract and should stay stable.

nezeri.q: What does idempotency mean in REST?
opts: Repeating the same request doesn't change the result
nezeri.exp: GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent. POST isn't — if you send it twice, two resources are created.

nezeri.q: Where should configuration (passwords, keys) be stored on a server?
opts: In environment variables or a secret manager
In plain text in the database
nezeri.exp: A secret stored in code ends up in the repo and stays in the history forever. Environment variables are the bare minimum.

nezeri.q: What does a plugin do in Ktor?
opts: It adds behavior to the request processing pipeline — JSON, logging, CORS, auth
nezeri.exp: Ktor consists of a minimal core. Every feature you need is installed explicitly as a plugin — nothing works behind your back.

nezeri.q: Should you choose Ktor or Spring for a new project?
opts: It depends on the project — Ktor for microservices and KMP, Spring for ready-made enterprise solutions
nezeri.exp: Ktor is lightweight and Kotlin-native. Spring, with its mature ecosystem, handles complex enterprise requirements out of the box.
